The proposed approach involves a new joint rain generation and removal model based on disentangled image translation, which is trained to decompose the image into rain and background images.  The model is then capable of reversing this decomposition to reconstruct the original image.  Experiments show that the proposed approach is capable of removing rain from real-world images with improved accuracy compared to existing techniques.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks.

We discuss recent research findings regarding model companions in set theory within the context of ongoing debates in the philosophy of mathematics. Initially, we explore how the concept of model companions is affected by the signature, before specifically examining the dependence of model companions in set theory. Our analysis indicates that the most intrinsic model companions for set theory correspond to $H_{\kappa^+}$ theories, as the infinite cardinal $\kappa$ varies. Furthermore, we investigate whether the Continuum problem has a model-theoretic underpinning related to the nature of model companions within set theory.
This study establishes conditions and proof of existence for a modified Branson-Paneitz equation under Navier boundary conditions on a finite region of n-dimensional Euclidean space.

Evaluating a person's risk of drug abuse is crucial, and online surveys have proven effective for gathering relevant data. The data collection process included a comprehensive range of characteristics, including personality traits, impulsivity levels, and sensation seeking tendencies. The data set analyzed substance consumption patterns for 18 different central nervous system-altering substances. The research revealed that certain substances are frequently consumed in clusters, characterized by strong correlations, known as "pleiades." Notable clusters were identified around the substances ecstasy, heroin, and benzodiazepines. By exploring various classification techniques and features, a data-driven approach identified the most effective methods to categorize individuals as users or non-users for each specific substance or cluster. Among the techniques examined, including tree models and probability estimations, a top-performing classifier was chosen for each drug. The accuracy of these classifications exceeded 70 percent for nearly all substances when using a rigorous evaluation method. The best performance was seen for the substances cannabis, crack, ecstasy, legal highs, LSD, and volatile substance abuse, achieving a high classification accuracy of above 75 percent.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.

Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the linear system of equations resulting from mean-variance portfolio optimization can be solved efficiently using quadratic convergence. However, even though quantum computers excel at solving linear systems, the native lack of conditional statements within quantum circuits presents an insurmountable barrier for the implementation of if-then statements in a portable manner across different quantum architectures. Furthermore, the vast disparity in asset prices necessitates an enormous number of digital annealing devices, an impractical requirement. To overcome these challenges, we propose an alternative approach based on the Hybrid Quantum-Classical Algorithm, combining the strengths of quantum simulation of linear systems and classical integer programming. By leveraging the capabilities of superposition computing, this approach yields a substantial increase in portfolio sizes that can be optimized on noise-tolerant quantum devices, specifically up to 10,000 assets with only 1024 digital annealing devices. Moreover, we demonstrate that our proposed approach matches the efficiency of the classical homogeneous interior point method (CHIPM) and outperforms it on quantum devices, achieving a significant increase in optimized portfolio returns. Through our research, we aim to pave the way for the integration of quantum computing into portfolio optimization, addressing the computational challenges faced by financial institutions with complex portfolios.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with linguistic information, while the language representations are infused with supplementary supplementary acoustic information. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant reduction in the word error rate (WER) and an enhancement in data efficiency. The results show that the proposed method offers a substantial 8.48% WER reduction when using a small dataset and a 6.89% improvement when the corpus is expanded with additional data.

This analysis addresses the challenge of optimizing cross-sectional area through a specific point within a geometric form. To generalize this concept, the approach is expanded across multiple dimensions. Nonetheless, the optimal average cross-sectional volume cannot be achieved unless cross-sections pass through the centroid of the shape. Therefore, the focus is on stationary shapes with optimal average cross-section properties. A new formula is introduced for average cross-section calculations in any dimension, and the associated equation of stationary shapes is derived. Characteristics of stationary shapes are discussed through mathematical derivation, numerical modeling, and graphical visualization. Additionally, the distinct properties of stationary shapes in 2D, 3D, and 5D are analyzed and explored.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, show significant conductance modulations in response to gate voltage, occurring when the voltage surpasses certain threshold values. The relationship between the measurements and the distance between the gate and the nanowires is the subject of the presented investigation. The study reveals that the conductance of the nanowires can be modulated using a gate made of semiconductor material, based on the tunneling effect, and that the coherence of quantum phase slips is evident from the observed hysteresis and start-up currents. The study also demonstrates that the blockade occurs when the charge accumulation across the nanowires matches specific integer values, and that the desorption of Cooper pairs is necessary for the phenomenon of quantum phase slip. The presented investigation offers a comprehensive understanding of the blockade and start-up currents in NbN nanowires and suggests that these features might be utilized in the detection of rare quantum events.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial evidence for the class's existence; however, the lack of precise spectral data regarding this body has sustained over the past two decades. Our study presents an innovative use of the APOLLO code, implementing a holistic approach to combine light curves and radial velocity data, enabling a comprehensive examination of GJ 229A's transit and activity. This study redesigns the orbit of GJ 229B based on new observational data from the SPITZER and VHS catalogs. Our analysis suggests a highly irregular spectral spectrum for GJ 229B, resolving previous discrepancies. We have derived various solar system analogues and exoplanets that exhibit similar infrared properties to GJ 229B across 3.0-4.2 μm. These findings indicate that infrared flux systems are not uncommon in low-mass stellar environments. Additionally, we have obtained an accurate temperature reading of around 882 K (0.79 ± 0.04) for GJ 229B, confirming various earlier spectral features. Its mass is estimated to be 29.8 ± 4.4 M$_{\oplus}$, slightly exceeding the minimum required for sustained hydrogen burning.

Our study offers an explanation of the structural properties of a thermal medium like quark-gluon plasma, using the framework of electron scattering via virtual photons on this medium. In particular, we investigate deep-inelastic scattering (DIS) processes and derive moment sum rules from structure functions. These sum rules can be expressed as the thermal expectation values of twist-two operators, and such calculations are feasible using lattice QCD for a small set of operators related to DIS at a scale relevant to physical observations. This involves a thermal evolution from the temperature to the observed values of kinematic variables in the data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the thermal evolution functions for the structure functions can be determined from the expectation values of the operators in the path integral approach. Alternatively, these evolution functions can also be found from the thermal Wilson coefficients in the operator product expansion, considering the dispersion relations for the structure functions in the form of thermal dispersion relations.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views.

In this research, inter-orbital coupling was demonstrated using femtosecond laser writing, which enables orthogonal modes in a photonic lattice to couple with each other at different spatial locations. We characterized an asymmetric double-well structure, mapped its propagation dynamics and successfully created a device capable of spatial mode conversion anywhere within a photonic chip. Utilizing higher-order photonic mode phase structure, our experiment showed that a trimer configuration can serve as a $\pi$-phase beam splitter for multiplexing and other interference-based photonic applications.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches and available experimental evidence.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the variability in the distribution of particles is found to be significantly influenced by the Reynolds number, often used as a basis for categorizing 'low' and 'high' turbulence levels; however, the commonly cited values for this parameter may not accurately capture the dynamics at play in bus transmissions.

Building on cutting-edge experimental projects such as HIBEF at the XFEL, our calculations investigate the birefringent scattering of x-rays when interacting with two combined optical lasers, considering various possible outcomes. To aid in detecting quantum vacuum effects experimentally, our analysis focuses particularly on situations where x-ray photons show differences not just in polarization, but also in direction of propagation and potential energy changes.

This note outlines the algorithm devised by J. M. Eisenlohr and S. L. Farris to
systematically generate all fully transitive polyhedra in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space. Furthermore, this algorithm is employed to construct a novel polyhedron within three-dimensional Euclidean space.

Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

  - Applications to Copy Protection: We've discovered that strong forms of unclonable encryption can lead to enhanced security, specifically copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Our research paves the way for potential new constructions meeting these requirements, thereby expanding the realm of copy-protection methods.

This study confirms that physical layer-based authentication is achievable in
Gaussian noise environments, with the caveat that an all-knowing adversary cannot be
beated. An examination of a model comprising encoder, decoder, and adversary was
carried out, with the latter possessing unlimited transmission capabilities and
unlimited access to the transmitted message. It was demonstrated that modifying an
existing communication protocol can enable secure transmission with negligible
efficiency loss, providing an attacker's knowledge does not equate to total access.
Notably, this technique does not rely on the specific characteristics of an attacker's
transmission and does not require a shared secret, thereby facilitating the
implementation of a secure and robust communication system. Furthermore, a secure
transmission capacity model was formulated and found to converge to standard
transmission capacity when no unauthorized access occurs. As a modular system,
this approach can be applied across multiple scenarios.

We utilized the full tight-binding model and random phase approximation to
explore flat-band plasmons in hole-doped twisted bilayer molybdenum disulfide.
Our calculations showed that lattice relaxation influences plasmon behavior.
When we considered intraband transitions, low-damped, flat plasmons emerged,
while accounting for interband transitions led to plasmon dispersion following
$\sqrt q$ law. The plasmon energies in these materials can be adjusted through
tweaking the twist angles and doping levels. For samples without lattice
relaxations, coexistence of low and high-energy plasmons occurs. Higher doping
levels however eliminate the quasi-flat plasmon. These observations imply that
two conditions must be satisfied: a flat band isolated from the other bands
and adequate doping level to witness the quasi-flat plasmon. The study offers
clues for exploring superconductivity mediated by plasmons in these materials.

This paper expresses the potential function $f$ associated with an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold in terms of the scalar field $p$, determining when the potential function is constant, and establishing a link between $f$ and $\lambda$. We also establish a condition for a conformal Ricci soliton to be a gradient Ricci soliton, and provide a characterization of the soliton in terms of its contraction or expansion rate.

Both celestial bodies can experience mass loss due to an expansive outward flow,
often regulated or redirected by magnetic fields that create a surrounding
magnetospheric field. Powerful star winds are generated by the scattering of the
star's radiative force, whereas in smaller stars and our Sun, weaker mass loss is
caused by thermal expansion of the mechanically heated outer layer. This process
can also occur in planets around low-mass stars, resulting in thermal expansion or
mechanical wear on their atmospheres. Magnetospheres in stars arise from wind flow
containment, whereas planetary magnetospheres are shaped by the external impact of
the star's wind. However, in both cases, magnetic reconnection due to the strain can
lead to detectable phenomena like X-ray flares and radio bursts. This review aims to
summarize the underlying physics of these processes and their shared and unique
aspects in stars and planets.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with another material. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity, attributed to the increase of Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and the Anomalous Hall Effect due to the Bi layer's influence. This effect is impaired by increasing Bi layer thickness, implying that the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect results from the Scattering of Bi carriers at the Cobalt interface.

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space and potential. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential returns to the original Mie-type form. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. Verification of results is achieved by comparison with existing studies. Numerical examples illustrating energy eigenvalue spectra and corresponding eigenfunction behaviour are presented for $\alpha=0.5$ and $\alpha=1.5$.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training with a restricted Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem with a penalty term, which can be resolved through stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained with low norms ($p=1$ or $p=2$) performed competitively with state-of-the-art methods for image classification, while also demonstrating the significance of the neural network's depth and width in relation to its Lipschitz constraint.

Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental questions regarding their capacity
to learn complex language hierarchies and grammatical patterns naturally
occurring in human language.
As a case study for understanding the implicit comprehension of sentence
structure and the adoption of a complex yet systematic morphological system,
we explore agreement prediction in Basque, which demands a thorough analysis
of both.
Our analysis of the results of verb number prediction and suffix recovery in
two experiments indicates that sequential models perform below expected levels
on the Basque agreement prediction compared to similar models tested with
English data.
Our exploratory findings based on diagnostic tools indicate that neural
networks may leverage local strategies to compensate for their limited grasp
of hierarchical sentence structures.
As such, we introduce a method for gauging the reliance of sequence models
on linear versus branching patterns.
Our approach and the associated code are available online at https://github.com/AntoniXanqui/LT-Model-Linear-vs-Branching.

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives due to its highly eccentric 111-day orbit. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is crucial to making the most out of these observations. Researchers have conducted in-depth analyses of the planet's transits on February 7, 2020, and December 7-8, 1998, along with a third, more recent observation reported by the TESS spacecraft. These findings, coupled with a third, more recent observation reported by the TESS spacecraft, have led to a refinement of the planet's orbital path and a small adjustment to its estimated mass. As a result, scientists have detected a subtle imbalance in the orbit they attribute to gravitational interactions with the host star, a phenomenon that causes slight variations in the time it takes the planet to complete one orbit. Researchers believe that the most efficient use of JWST observations would be to study the planet as it approaches its star, a process that takes approximately 36 days.

Customized digital games successfully encourage motivation in repetitive exercises required for motor rehabilitation; nevertheless, developing adjustments that cater to both therapy and enjoyment objectives poses a challenge. To tackle this issue, we propose an approach where an initial statistical model of game performance identifies specific settings that mirror players' typical behavior, even in the face of diminished control. This approach is exemplified through a practical application involving upper limb rehabilitation and a specially designed controller for the Pac-Man game. Collaborative sessions between occupational therapists and game developers resulted in the identification of two key factors that affect the gameplay experience and influence rehabilitation adjustments. Experimental measurements of the participants' interaction with the modified game revealed that our low-latency statistical model accurately identifies optimal parameter values that reproduce baseline gameplay under controlled conditions. This methodology holds potential for addressing balance problems related to the design of gamified systems, particularly those involving conflicting requirements for physical involvement and subjectively enjoyable experiences.

Our research offers a variational approximation, drawing from the Ambrosio-Tortorelli model, to quantify brittle fracture energies in complex, piecewise-rigid structures, applicable to both nonlinear and linearised elasticity frameworks.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework, one component of which is inspired by the theory of robustness for neural networks evaluating probability distributions, enables the training of a model that generates high-quality PET images from low-dose PET and MRI scans with associated side information, in addition to yielding a rating of uncertainty for the new acquisitions outside of its distribution. The model's ability to generalize to new acquisitions outside of its distribution is demonstrated through experiments with real data, showing that deep learning can enhance PET images despite significantly lower doses and varying demographic characteristics.

The issue of tailoring news to individuals' interests based on their browsing history, in order to keep them engaged, is examined from both a business and a user perspective. The benefits of personalized content are discussed, but the potential drawbacks, including loss of privacy and biased information, are also highlighted. The problem with the endless pursuit of user data and revenue is the inherent conflict between media companies' commercial goals and users' need for trustworthy and diverse information. The need for transparent and optional personalized services, as well as initiatives that promote high-quality, fact-based news, are stressed.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it better captures the connections within the text compared to the original CT.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs.

The rising intricacy of modern adaptable systems demands elevated automation in their configuration process, thus also accelerating development cycles via rapid, automated workflow integration. A novel automated configuration framework is introduced, using model checking and SMT, adaptable to any domain definable by SMT formulas, allowing for modular scalability and improved human understanding via metric-driven optimization. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to configuring a CGRA memory tile for diverse image processing tasks.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. Specifically, we investigate the trailing entanglement spectrum, trailing entanglement probability distribution, and effective trailing correlation length in $su(1,1)$ and $su(N)$ systems. Our findings reveal that the operator growth phenomenon exhibits universal characteristics in line with a power-law behavior, with key parameters (such as the correlation length and specific ratios of them) determined by the Lie algebra in question. Notably, certain systems within this category, such as the $su(1,1)$ breast system, display operator growth patterns identical to those found in the Lie-symmetric free fermion model. Nonetheless, we have encountered instances (e.g., $su(N)$ hydrodynamic modes) where the operator growth phenomenon is fully captured by a logarithmic law, a feature not observable in the Lie-symmetric free fermion model. Our research paves the way for a broader exploration of operator growth within self-dual quantum many-body systems, incorporating concepts from conformal field theory.

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the chosen metric and often falls short of accurate results. To address this challenge, the study proposes utilizing supervised machine learning to enhance the estimation of distances between these data sets. The experimental findings, conducted in a university library, demonstrate that employing supervised machine learning techniques leads to significantly more precise results, outperforming the conventional Euclidean distance by a margin of more than two times when using the RMS error as the performance metric.

For nearly 60 years, researchers have been searching for signs of extraterrestrial life through SETI initiatives, with a Dyson Sphere as a primary target - an advanced megastructure capable of harnessing a star's energy for an advanced civilization. A study explores whether constructing such a structure around a black hole would be feasible and efficient in powering a civilization. Considering six potential energy sources, researchers found that an accretion disk, which can produce $10^{5}\,{\rm L_{\odot}}$ of energy, would be sufficient for an advanced civilization. Additionally, a Dyson Sphere could potentially collect energy from relativistic jets and increase its overall energy output fivefold. Calculations indicate that a Dyson Sphere constructed around a stellar-mass black hole in the Milky Way could be detectable with current telescopes using waste heat radiation in the ultraviolet to mid-infrared spectrum. Analyzing spectral energy distributions and radial velocity variations could aid in identifying possible artificial structures, such as Dyson Spheres.

Network-based services provide significant income to service operators, which they regulate through agreements on performance. Ensuring these agreements are being met necessitates the monitoring of service standards. A method to accomplish this involves deploying active measurement tools, which send test traffic and gauge performance. Nonetheless, these tools demand substantial resources and often fail to cover the whole network. Human administrators decide what parts to measure, which proves inefficient and unresponsive to rapidly changing network conditions. This article discusses the advantages of employing peer-to-peer (P2P) technology to enhance the identification of SLA breaches. Initially, we explore the principles of steering active measurement tools via P2P. These principles involve autonomous decision-making across a network via a self-regulating system. Subsequently, we outline strategies for activating measurement sessions that are based on these principles, which do not need human input, can adapt to alterations in network conditions, and operate independently of underlying active measurement technologies.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs.

To determine the parameters for neutrino oscillation, cutting-edge experiments employing long-baseline neutrino detection systems rely heavily on the development of detailed models describing the interactions between neutrinos and atomic nuclei. The intricacy of these models is significant, partly because existing detectors have been incapable of observing final state neutrons, which has led to significant systematic uncertainties. The implementation of 3D scintillator tracking technology in next-generation long-baseline neutrino experiments has improved detection capabilities by enabling event-by-event measurement of neutron kinetic energy resulting from neutrino interactions, thus providing valuable information for refining neutrino interaction models and reconstructing neutrino energies. Prototypes of these detectors have undergone neutron irradiation at the LANL beamline in both 2019 and 2020. The primary goal was to demonstrate the ability of neutron detection by comparing the total cross-sectional area of neutrons and scintillator interaction at 98-688 MeV, which was measured at 0.36±0.05 barn, in accordance with established external measurement standards.

In a previous series of experiments, we discovered how sticking forces changed in response to temperature among particles made of chondritic materials, which indicated that their surface energy drops by approximately 5 times when temperatures rise. In the present investigation, we shift focus to the effect of surface moisture on the grains under normal lab conditions, which involves having multiple water layers. In the case of the cooler protoplanetary discs and moderate temperatures, grains likely only hold one water layer. Since this water layer would evaporate in the warmer sections of the discs, we conducted experiments at two temperatures (around 100 and 300 degrees Celsius) to gauge the impact on the grains' sticking properties when they possess this single water layer. The outcome showed that the higher temperature significantly lessened the sticking force, which in turn was found to be heavily dependent on the temperature rather than any influence of the water layer. Consequently, in our follow-up modeling, the inner 5 millimeters of each grain is treated as being in a separate thermal equilibrium due to its reduced sticking force, which is in line with the population breakdown observed in the MMHL particles.

Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) is a localized adaptation of the traditional Fisher Discriminant Analysis, widely employed for supervised dimensionality reduction techniques. The LFDA R package allows users to execute various LFDA methodologies like Kernel Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis and Semi-Supervised Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis. The package also facilitates dimensionality reduction result visualization, utilizing 3D (rgl) and 2D (ggfortify in ggplot2) graphical tools.

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness in complex scenarios involving nonlinear hard constraints, target reaching with end-effector grasping, and obstacle avoidance tasks.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of the NNLL CEV in $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM theory was previously found to exhibit a non-trivial dependence on the emission angle. Building on that result, we now determine the imaginary part of the NNLL CEV, which when combined with the dispersive part, enables a full understanding of the NNLL CEV in $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM theory. Consequently, we find the NNLL BFKL equation can be expressed in a factorizable form in impact parameter space. This development implies the NNLL BFKL equation can be solved via iterative methods, yielding actionable insights for quantifying NNLL accuracy in the color-dipole picture.

A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. However, obtaining spin-singlet $p$-wave superconductivity in these systems is challenging due to the competing effects of the Zeeman field and Rashba interaction, which tend to drive magnetic order. Employing the Rashba Hubbard model on a honeycomb lattice at half-filling and subject to an attractive interaction and weak Zeeman field, our calculations using the mean-field approximation and Monte Carlo simulations reveal that Rashba-induced ferromagnetism is counterbalanced by strong long-range interactions, giving rise to spin-singlet $d$-wave superconductivity instead. Furthermore, this result is unaffected by the specific layout of the lattice, and we find that the competition between Rashba-induced ferromagnetism and long-range interactions allows for the emergence of the desired spin-singlet $p$-wave state by adjusting the Rashba interaction strength.

By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure of the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. The discovered phase shift, occurring at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point without magnetic field, can be identified by measuring the stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice, at a doping concentration of $x=p=0.17$. Our theoretical calculations using the Eilenberger theory for interlocked vortices demonstrate that this transition represents the expected rotation of the square lattice structure by 45 degrees predicted for materials that are $d$-wave superconductors near a point of high singularity.

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying a distinct end exclusion zone and offering a precise description of brush height in relation to the curve's radius of curvature. This advancement paves the way for a deeper understanding of block copolymer morphologies and surface-adhesion behaviors, and we anticipate that our findings will also be instrumental in optimizing ellipsoidal nanoparticle synthesis.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations.

Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on the hardness of optimizing serial dictatorships for specific action sequences, particularly focusing on graph-related problems like Maximum Matching, Maximum Independent Set, and Minimum Vertex Cover. We also explore the applicability of our results to combinatorial optimization challenges within the broader framework of multi-agent optimization frameworks.

We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4.1 < g' < 6.5. Although the method showed effectiveness in identifying 
single asteroids, it struggled to detect binary asteroids. To improve the 
method's sensitivity, we implemented various optimization strategies, 
including smoothing the PSF data, utilizing the Galfit3 program, and 
constrained fittings. Even with these adjustments, the method remained 
ineffective in identifying binary asteroids. The algorithm's primary 
limitation appears to be the inability to distinguish between the central 
point spread function of a binary system and that of a solitary asteroid, 
given that the separation between the components of the binary system exceeds 
the PSF radius. To enhance the method's sensitivity, we need to develop a 
more sophisticated understanding of point spread functions in Pan-STARRS1 images 
or utilize context-provided asteroid parameters for a more targeted search.

This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Auerbach in 2019. The paper's first section explores the asymptotic behavior of the estimators presented in section 2 of the Auerbach's work. The second section investigates extensions to the model. The third section applies the model to estimate peer effects within networks. The fourth section presents results obtained from simulated data.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, four quotient rule formulas derived from product rule types, and four chain rule formulas have been established.

This paper analyzes the performance of complex MIMO systems that utilize spatial modulation and multiuser detection with a least-squares method, and derives rate and distortion metrics for this setup. By applying an asymptotic characterization, we evaluate specific detector methods, including an optimal Bayesian detector, and develop a simplified approach for optimizing a related detection method, before supporting our findings with numerical simulations.

We've developed an open-source suite of web visualization tools tailored for
analyzing spectral and imaging data, which are being utilized in the second edition
of the RCSED galaxy energy distribution catalog (rcsed2.voxastro.org). To create
these tools, we employed Quasar and Vue.js web technologies to build engaging,
interactive viewers for visualizing galaxy spectra, SEDs, and diagnostic diagrams,
such as BPT diagrams generated from spectroscopic analysis. Leveraging client-side
processing via JavaScript minimizes server load, while maintaining seamless user
interactivity. Additionally, the adoption of modern web frameworks facilitates
extensive customization, making our visualization tools effortlessly integratable
into astronomical database websites and databases. Furthermore, this framework is
also compatible with Aladin Lite and other popular third-party web tools.

The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that the rifting accelerations in West Africa and Brazil occurred 134 ± 5 cm/y and 130 ± 5 cm/y respectively, with the rifting directions shifting from ENE in Brazil to NE in West Africa, corresponding to a rifting angle of approximately 20°.  This difference is attributed to pre-rift continental deformation linked to the Gondwana supercontinent.  Rifting in Brazil started around 135 Ma, preceded by very slow extensional deformation beginning around 140 Ma, while in West Africa, rifting commenced around 125 Ma, preceded by 25 Ma of stable crust.  Based on finite strain analysis and 2D/3D numerical modeling, the break-up velocities were estimated at 134 ± 5 cm/y in Central and West Africa and 130 ± 5 cm/y in Brazil.  The time elapsed between the onset of rifting and break-up in both regions was around 25 million years.  This research provides new insights into the post-rift evolution of the conjugate Brazilian and West African margins, challenging the previous theory that break-up occurred

A proven strategy to enhance multiple tasks with limited labeled data is
unsupervised pre-training.  Despite being a viable approach, contrastive
learning poses challenges in forming relevant pairs for an unsupervised
segmentation task. To circumvent these challenges, our proposed framework
utilizes two primary components:  using unsupervised over-segmentation with
mutual information maximization and a pre-training task.  The experimental
results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in enhancing
segmentation performance on real-world medical image segmentation tasks.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context.

Despite significant research on Lexical Semantic Change Detection, most approaches remain limited to standard model assessments. This study deviates from this focus, shifting towards change discovery - identifying previously unknown word meanings emerging over time within a comprehensive corpus vocabulary. By extensively leveraging paradigmatic and syntagmatic information from a corpus and a lexical database, our method pinpoints emerging words by analyzing their co-occurring language patterns and categorization across periods. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by discovering new words with a high degree of accuracy compared to existing detection methods and even excel in tasks like semantic relatedness and sentence completion. However, the system faces difficulties with inflectional words and those requiring context to understand their full meaning.

We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. Additionally, they depend on the transverse momentum of the parton in the hadron's rest frame, distinctively capturing $k_\perp$ dependencies observed in data. Using a effective field theory, saturation dynamics are utilized with the Chiral Path Quark (CPQ) model to gain insight into these functions and how they relate to quark spin alignment, $k_\perp$ distributions, and azimuthal modulations in particle production processes.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations.

To resolve the discrepancy known as the Hubble tension, early dark energy (EDE) has been proposed. Although researchers agree on the existence of EDE, its properties remain unclear. By analyzing the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's large-scale structure, we discovered varying results due to limitations of current constraints, specifically volume effects that influence model parameter choices. Employing an unbiased statistical analysis technique called a profile likelihood to assess EDE parameters, we determined a confidence interval of $f_\mathrm{EDE} = 0.072\pm 0.036$ ($68\%$ C.L.), providing a clearer picture of EDE and its potential solution to the Hubble tension.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite.

A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can give rise to a nonrelativistic long-distance approximation of the effective potential similar to that derived in the 1970s by Salam and others. A specific example of symmetry breaking with a complex scalar field within a nonrelativistic effective potential framework has been examined. Furthermore, the connection between the anomalous NG theorem and the Coleman-Mann theorem has been established through an example involving a real scalar field. A discussion on the physical implications of the anomalous NG theorem has been provided, addressing the emergence of mass scales, the generation of massless modes, and the existence of long-lived phenomena associated with the anomalous NG theorem. In addition, we consider the theoretical framework that underpins modern understanding of the universe, the Standard Model, in light of the anomalous NG theorem.

Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to generalize across categories. However, the limitations of current methods in generating high-quality counterfactuals on a large scale hinder the full realization of their potential. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel framework called DISCO that enables the production of a vast quantity of counterfactual data at a relatively low cost. This framework distills a large language model with the ability to produce phrasal counterfactuals by first training a compressor model that reduces the complexity of the model's parameters and then a target model that generates counterfactuals with the compressed representations. Through our experiments on supervised learning tasks, we found that the counterfactuals generated by our method are accurate and effective in producing a significant improvement in performance. Moreover, our method is cost-effective in producing a large amount of counterfactual data, leading to an even more substantial gain in performance.

In this study, we determined the total chromatic numbers along with their equitable and
neighborhood sum distinguishing counterparts for specific types of circulant graphs.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene can recover its full conductivity, enabling the successful growth of Pinhole and van der Waals epitaxy GdPtSb layers.

A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that has properties derived from $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code, given a prime number p greater than two. This paper specifically delves into the examination of the rank and dimension of the kernel of these $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes. Furthermore, specific limits on the rank of $\Z_3 \Z_9$-linear codes and the dimension of the kernel of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes have been established and detailed examples are provided.

The technology of graded viscosity banks, specifically tapering for polymer flooding,
has been analyzed using various models of mixing zone behavior. By considering different
viscosity functions, researchers have mathematically determined the optimal polymer injection
profile, given transverse flow equilibrium assumptions, for both the Koval and Todd-Longstaff models.
Moreover, a numerical assessment has been conducted to evaluate potential polymer gains relative
to flooding using a finite number of polymer slugs.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting where training data is only labeled with a single positive label, but allows for the generation of a broader range of classes, resulting in significant reductions in annotation costs.  A new technique, unsupervised sample selection, is introduced to generate diverse high-quality samples from this dataset, allowing for the conditional GAN to learn multiple labels with ease.  The proposed method is compared to traditional multi-label training methods, revealing that it yields a notable improvement in performance.

This study investigates the property of energy dissipation associated with the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation, introducing an upper bound that decreases over time, aligns with the original energy at time zero, and remains finite for all positive times. The upper bound is expressed as a convolution term involving the Caputo kernel and the initial energy. The novelty of this research lies in its verification of the upper bound, which holds for the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation with a nonhomogeneous boundary condition and even allows for a substantial increase in energy due to the memory effect of the fractional derivative. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the energy upper bound converges to the original energy as the memory of the fractional derivative fades away.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms.

The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies at gamma-ray frequencies, we found that it can account for radiation in the higher energy bands.  However, a different, more powerful source is required to explain gamma-rays in the lower energy band.  This source could be massive binary systems or the pair of a supermassive black hole and a less massive compact object.  The same analysis also showed that the MAD model is consistent with observations of two binary systems featuring a black hole and a neutron star or a white dwarf, as their gamma-ray spectra were formed by the high-energy radiation of the surrounding environment rather than the emission from the binary system itself.

This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model portfolio returns, establishing essential formulas and efficient algorithms using techniques from computational geometry and splines. By leveraging these methods, our approach can efficiently handle large portfolios and accurately compute moments of the distribution of returns using methods such as the Delta method. We have developed specific formulas for key statistics, including the skewness and semi-deviation of the returns, and demonstrated the applicability of our framework to real-world scenarios through case studies.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique achieves the best results across a wide range of recording conditions and environments, indicating its potential for low-cost implementation.  The findings provide a framework for creating cardiac auscultation systems capable of accurately diagnosing conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. To address these issues, we introduce FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare capable of processing cross-device and cross-user data transfer learning. FedHealth encompasses not only traditional federated learning but also a range of advanced transfer learning techniques including domain adaptation, transfer learning, and meta-learning. Furthermore, FedHealth incorporates versatile wearable data preprocessing and visualization features alongside diverse healthcare applications. The framework is available online at https://github.com/hjdwsg/FedHealth, enabling the creation of cutting-edge healthcare applications and facilitating collaborative research among academics and industry professionals in the field of wearable healthcare.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations.

In string compactifications, we suggest that dark energy marks the universe's end, 
potentially triggered by decompactification, addressing the cosmological coincidence issue. 
Lack of stable de Sitter vacua forces us to model dark energy as a slow-rolling quintessence field. 
This process inevitably leads to a chaotic, universe-altering phase shift, likely after several hundred 
cosmological time cycles. Dark energy dominance, therefore, cannot persist forever, and the chance 
exists that we reside in the universe's first epoch. Our quintessence model illustrates the 
dysfunctional universe dynamics resulting from the descent of heavy states, when a multitude of particles 
are produced, overshadowing the quintessence's power. Additionally, our theory raises implications 
for the universe's early inflationary periods.

In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing a substantial number of applicants, a time-consuming and intricate process. To achieve efficiency, a well-planned approach to selection is crucial. This process comprises multiple, interconnected problems, each mirroring a well-known computational issue. While individual research has been extensively conducted, an integrated examination of these problems is uncommon. This paper addresses two critical aspects of application processing: creating review and interview panels and scheduling interviews. We developed a prototype system to automate interview planning for a real-world scenario. Compared to existing, manual methods, our approach yields a superior plan. To achieve this, we evaluated different algorithmic options and tailored them to solve panel creation and scheduling issues. We experimented with these solutions using real data, presenting our findings. This study may serve as a starting point for further development aimed at fully automating application processing processes.

This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies that minimize costs under this dynamic framework. Alongside, we examine the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to a system of stochastic differential equations featuring abrupt obstacles, whose characteristics depend on the unknown solution. Finally, the paper also considers the case when the underlying system includes a random movement, resulting in the optimal payoff becoming a solution to a quasi-variational HJB PDE system with discontinuous barriers. This research is an extension of prior works on smooth costs in references [8, 17].

To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates asymmetric leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and aid in identifying its potential. Asymmetric production stands out from conventional methods as leptoquarks created in proton-proton collisions aren't opposite charges. To make this process possible, we outline the required conditions and list all relevant combinations of leptoquark groups that can create it. Furthermore, our studies in the Standard Model and its scalar extensions demonstrate how to integrate this process into reinterpretations of existing experiments, producing more accurate leptoquark property constraints.

Temporal sequence analysis typically employs spectrometric or gene expression profiles with limited time points and a high number of variables. Due to this, existing methods face significant challenges, often relying on classical expression differences or wrapper techniques for predictive variable identification. A key issue lies in the small sample size common in such studies. In contrast, our proposed supervised learning approach, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time, successfully tackles these challenges by creating a low-dimensional grid mapping for temporal sequences. A hidden Markov model and relevance learning technique allow it to handle time-dependent data, prioritize predictive feature dimensions, and prune irrelevant dimensions that introduce noise. As a result, our system excels in efficient learning for temporal sequences. Compared to conventional techniques, incorporating simultaneous supervised learning and model-based time course analysis yields superior results in benchmark datasets and the prediction of adaptive responses in rat liver primary cultures exposed to toxic substances.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which data is available for two specific fine structure lines of neutral atomic carbon, and we found their average conditions to be unusually uncommon. Typically, these lines are linked to energy levels that are significantly populated by temperatures greater than 100 Kelvin, yet in our sample, temperatures are around 50 Kelvin. This discrepancy holds true even when considering gas temperatures observed in other molecular gas observations. We found no clear connection between the carbon lines and other galaxy properties such as star formation rate or molecular gas mass. However, we noticed a potential correlation with gas velocity, and since these lines are sensitive to small-scale gas motion, they could be a useful indicator of molecular gas dynamics, especially when optical observations are not feasible.

We tackle current, striking discrepancies in flavor anomalies observed within the $K$ and $B$ meson systems, specifically addressing CP-violating Kaon decay and lepton-flavor universality violation in $B$ meson decays, with the latter including events involving muons decaying into electrons, a process known as $R_K$ and $R_{K^*}$, and another involving a hadronic process known as $R_{D(\tau)}$ and $R_{D^* (\tau)}$. To resolve these anomalies, we employ vectorlike compositeness, a theory that adds vector boson couplings to flavons (Higgs-like particles) at a scale of $\Lambda$ which lies between 1 TeV and 5 TeV, a range that results from combining anomalies with contributions from a fifth dimension, via Kaluza-Klein states. This compositeness model naturally explains the anomalies at tree level, and despite contributing to a negative shift in the $K^0$-$\overline{K^0}$ mass difference, avoids conflict with lattice QCD simulations. Furthermore, we find that this model fails to meet experimental standards for CP non-leptonic Kaon decay when the underlying theory is an extension of the Standard Model, but it does meet requirements for a fifth-dimensional type of theory that employs a fifth-dimensional "warped" model.

Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the Hamming distance between two sequences of
characters is measured, and the goal is to determine the original sequence
based on a set of distorted versions of that sequence, with each distorted
version representing a permutation of the sequence's characters after a certain
distance. This problem has been extensively explored in fields like computer science
and genetics. However, all existing research on this topic has been limited to
sequences with the Levenshtein distance, which considers the replacement of
characters as well as their distortion. In contrast, the present study focuses
on permutations of the original sequence with the Hamming distance, and it presents
a new approach that involves upper and lower bounds on the number of distorted
versions required to reconstruct the original sequence. It also provides specific
reconstruction criteria for certain numbers of distorted versions.

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition or removal of categories. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our proposed method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that weren't encountered during training.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, as evaluated through human-and machine-generated answer pairs and information retrieval experiments.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits.
