To effectively manage the vast amounts of data generated by a growing number of IoT devices and emerging applications, future 5G networks must be able to dynamically adjust and prioritize traffic. By integrating artificial potential fields and a multi-agent system into the 5G RAN, future cellular networks can self-organize and optimize performance in real-time, ensuring efficient resource utilization and minimizing latency. This approach enables 5G networks to seamlessly adapt to changing traffic patterns and enable services such as massive machine-type communications, massive data transfers, and low-latency applications like remote surgery and virtual reality.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on specific instances of these problems, yet a comprehensive solution eluded them. In contrast, the current paper provides a general solution to problem 1 for metric spaces with angle functions, while also offering a solution to problem 2 in the context of semi-metric spaces with angle functions.

Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves, examining the interplay between minima and other geometric invariants.

We utilize a 1-d fs/ps hybrid technique in dual-probe rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy (CARS) to achieve direct, simultaneous single-shot measurements of temperature, pressure, and O2/N2 composition in the gas phase. With the fs probe, we obtain high-resolution O2 and N2 rotational spectra to determine the respective temperatures and oxygen concentrations via equilibrium relationships and quantum mechanics, while the ps probe yields pressure information through excitation of air's collective spectrum at an appropriate delay. The method demonstrates precise measurements of temperature (~43 K), pressure (~50 mbar), and oxygen concentration (1 part per million) in a test chamber. The method's efficiency and accuracy are showcased by monitoring the thermodynamic and chemical changes during the evaporation of a water droplet. The technique offers a versatile, compact, and user-friendly solution for the direct, simultaneous measurement of temperature, pressure, and gas composition in the field.

The traditional theory of planetary formation through core accretion has limitations when explaining how small particles overcome early development obstacles in a protoplanetary disk. A more recent model proposes the viscous ring-instability to account for ring structures in protoplanetary disks. It suggests that particles may reduce the disk's conductivity, inhibiting the growth of instability. Using GPU-based simulations of interacting gas and dust, this study investigates this model's validity. As the disk evolves, ring structures become unstable, breaking into smaller whirlpools, and subsequently forming stable dust formations. These structures provide ideal environments for the growth of planetary building blocks through gravitational collapse and the streaming instability. Observational data on exoplanets supports this process and creates favorable conditions for planetary system formation.

Quantum Hall phases exhibit gapped behavior in the interior while supporting both chiral and neutral edge modes.  A specific setup involving a path that only includes neutral modes, essential for an electric current from the source to the drain, is examined here. When a source is biased in this circuit, it is observed that an electric current can be measured at the drain, provided that backscattering between opposing modes at the contact locations is present. The result shows that neutral modes hold relevant information and can be used for a nonlocal reconstruction of a dc charge current. The described protocol may be employed to detect any neutral mode that counter-propagates with respect to charge modes, and this detection approach is applicable not only to the edge modes of quantum Hall systems but also to systems possessing neutral modes that do not originate from quantum Hall effects. Finally, an experimental demonstration of this concept is proposed for the edge electral of quantum Hall systems.

We introduce a rigid cluster model to achieve a representation of the quantum group U_q(g) for Lie algebras of type ADE. This involves establishing a natural isomorphism from the quantum group U_q(g) to a subalgebra within the quotient of Weyl group invariants from the Fock-Goncharov quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘). Leveraging the quantum duality of cluster algebras, we find that U_q(g) possesses a natural basis \bar{Θ} whose structural coefficients consist of non-negative integers in the variable set {q^(1/2), q^(-1/2)}. Furthermore, the basis \bar{Θ} maintains an invariance property under the braid group action defined by Lusztig, Dynkin's automorphisms, and the star anti-involution.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices.

This paper delves into the early days of computer simulations for hard-disk systems, tracing back to 1953 when Fernbach proposed using Monte Carlo methods to study these systems. However, the first notable attempt in this field was made by Metropolis and colleagues in 1953-1954, who indeed simulated hard-disk systems, though with a significant discrepancy in their findings resulting from an incorrect counting technique. Later, in the 1960s, the field saw significant advancements with the development of molecular dynamics and event-driven simulations, leading to a more precise understanding of hard-disk dynamics. Notably, the famous freezing transition in two-dimensional hard-disk systems was first observed in 1980 by Hoye and Lebowitz through Monte Carlo simulations, with the issue of whether this transition occurs within the simulation's accessible path also being discussed. Since then, simulations have continually revealed new aspects of hard-disk physics, with some questions still awaiting answer.

This paper examines jet modifications within a medium using JEWEL and PYTHIA 6.4, emphasizing uncertainties associated with perturbative scales, nuclear PDFs, and temperature variations of the medium at onset and transition points. Jet spectrum and nuclear modification factor data from the LHC are used for comparison with simulated results. Additionally, the influence of nuclear PDFs and the medium on jet structure is investigated through Lund plane analysis, and the interaction between nuclear PDF choice and medium parameters is explored.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages

A set of precise theoretical and experimental benchmarks at hadron colliders are based on color-singlet differential spectra, known as exclusive differential spectra. Our study provides a comprehensive effective-theory framework, using soft-collinear effective theory to account for heavy-quark effects in differential distributions at various scale hierarchies, specifically considering the splitting of a heavy quark in motion. This research extends a previous investigation by incorporating a leading-order scattering process and a leading logarithmic accuracy in renormalization and threshold, as well as incorporating a leading logarithmic accuracy in rapidity. It also facilitates the implementation of soft-function contributions that arise from multiple soft gluon interactions. To illustrate its relevance, we examine differential distributions for gamma* production at large rapidities (large-mass scales) within the PHENOMENON event generator, comparing the results from our effective-theory framework to those from the event generator. Our study provides a clear understanding of the theoretical uncertainties associated with quark effects and suggests a viable extension to the LHC, allowing for direct quark-effect measurements that would significantly beyond current sensitivity limits of LHC experiments with heavy-quark flavors.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model connected to the vector potential. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm models of photocatalysis and superconducting phases. Our analysis demonstrates that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description of electromagnetic fields and interacting systems, while the velocity-based model may lead to inaccuracies when relying on a long-wavelength approximation. Furthermore, both models fail to maintain gauge invariance when used individually, whereas the combination of the dipole-based electric field and velocity-based approach for the wave vector does preserve gauge invariance, providing a viable framework for simulations of optoelectronic properties within tight-binding models.

In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss, and accurately describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors. A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and possessing erasure correction capabilities can't simultaneously possess certain desirable traits - those that facilitate the efficient calculation of physical properties through a local process and those necessary for accurately describing phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors in their physical properties. This contradiction motivates the creation of network guidelines that utilize diverse types of tensors, allowing these networks to successfully capture the characteristics of power-law behaviors while adhering to the principle of efficient calculation. A concrete example of such a network has also been developed - one that closely resembles the holographic HaPPY pentagon code under the assumption that specific system parameters can be set to a particular small range.

A theoretical analysis of retinal chromophore photoisomerization in rhodopsin utilized a model incorporating thermal baths and dual states. It was observed that quantum yields in a steady-state condition (occurring 10 ps after the reaction begins and onwards) differ notably from their short-lived counterparts, indicating an imperfect correlation between transient and sustained behaviors. Furthermore, the steady-state quantum yield was shown to be exquisitely sensitive to minor adjustments in system parameters, in stark contrast to the relative insensitivity of transient dynamics. Analysis of this sensitivity in relation to nonadiabatic vibronic level spacing suggests that quantum chaos might underlie this phenomenon, and potential avenues for experimental validation along with implications in complex light-sensitive systems are explored.

Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determined by event quantities and case
completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior and
performance under different process conditions. Our experiments surprisingly
show that the basic Multi-layer Perceptron often achieves the best results, which
we attribute to the inherent order of process events, which facilitates the
use of sequential techniques like Temporal Multi-task Learning. To support our
findings, we offer a supplementary analysis highlighting model performances
across various process characteristics. To facilitate reproducibility and future
research, we present our data and implementation as an open-source
supplementation.

Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective crisis information dissemination. Social media can provide valuable insights into public perception, beneficial for crisis communication and management. This study focuses on analyzing Twitter posts related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake, aiming to leverage these insights to infer real-time public opinions. Utilizing a data set containing more than 183,000 tweets collected within a day of the earthquake, we employed various preprocessing techniques to extract meaningful information. Subsequently, we applied feature extraction and reduction to model users' behavior on Twitter. Ultimately, we used machine learning algorithms to classify users into two categories based on their earthquake-related tweets: those who posted relief messages and those who did not. The analysis revealed the superiority of certain features over others and compared the performance of different classification algorithms. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of reducing data dimensions on classification results.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The space ${\Sigma}^1_1$ is found to consist of periodic functions, while ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$ with $s \geq 1$ and ${\sigma} \geq 1$ forms a Banach space structure. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between these spaces and the Toeplitz operators with rough initial conditions.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of spectral energy distributions or full spectral observations during stellar flares. This research presents a computational approach to modeling the near-ultraviolet continuum of solar-like stars during flares using the CHIANTI database of spectral lines, the Grid-Based Model, and the AD Leo flare spectrum. The study specifically applies this model to the 1985 April 12 great flare of AD Leo, and the results show that it yields a reliable continuum model, integrating the flux to match observations in the GALEX UV band. This model has a sensitivity to electron density but is less affected by other variables such as the location of the emission, the temperature of the core, and the fraction of non-thermal energy. The models highlight the significance of magnetic field strength and non-thermal energy fraction in determining the flux of UV continuum during flares. This research offers a theoretical foundation for future missions like UVIST and HUBS that aim to observe white-light flares and starlight in the near-UV, and the approach developed here is applicable to grid searching and other Bayesian optimization methods.

This investigation into the PT-symmetric waveguide network's behavior uses mathematical models to derive exact equations describing wave propagation in a finite number of connected units. Analyzing this through generalized parametric space, researchers discovered that when PT symmetry breaks, propagating modes appear consistently across the unit cell and at the symmetry breaking point, especially in uniformly non-reciprocal systems. However, at the PT breaking point without breakdown, transparency is achieved only in certain correlated mode combinations. Additionally, CPAL can occur in PT-symmetric units connected in a specific way that allows for the conversion of time-reversed modes into each other.

We study the behavior and evolution of Boolean networks with sparse connections that interact with themselves using Glauber dynamics. These networks, which represent a system where variables influence each other and themselves through nonlinear interactions, evolve dynamically. We investigate how the dynamics are affected by the number of interacting variables, whether the network has an even or odd number of interacting variables, and whether variables interact with themselves. We find that the number of interacting variables significantly impacts the dynamics. For a large number of interacting variables, the dynamics is closely linked to the behavior of the network in equilibrium. However, for a small number of interacting variables, the dynamics is more complex, and intermediate dynamics emerges due to the interplay between attracting fixed points and chaotic dynamics. Moreover, we discover that the capacity for information processing is maximized when the network has an odd number of interacting variables and that self-interactions generally enhance the capacity, except in balanced capacitive networks. Furthermore, we find that the critical transition between order and chaos occurs when the number of attracting fixed points drops to zero, and this transition is induced by second-order phase transitions at specific driving forces.

We derive concise mathematical expressions for calculating matrix elements of single-particle and particle-particle operators that can be applied to a wide range of Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wave functions, encompassing configurations involving multiple quasiparticle excitations. Furthermore, our test simulations demonstrate the significant potential of these formulas to streamline the restoration of symmetry within large and complex nuclear systems.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional transformations. We then outline a universal protection method for all transformation categories by leveraging our previously developed method for shearable transformations and proving that rotating and stretching transformations share comparable vulnerability characteristics with abstractive transformation-based attacks. Consequently, our technique provides robust protection against all frequent three-dimensional attacks with a relatively light computational cost, achieving a notable trade-off between security and performance. Experimental results show that TPC achieves an average accuracy of 92.3% on the ModelNet40 dataset, a notable decline of only 3.5% in comparison to the baseline model.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We're developing and evaluating ALOHA and CSMA protocols to minimize the impact of narrowband interference, introducing a new metric to gauge performance based on network throughput. In the case of ALOHA, we analyze the probabilities of interference and system efficiency under different system parameters. We observe that FMCW network behavior diverges from typical wireless communication patterns. In some scenarios, increased packet transmission can decrease interference probabilities. We introduce a clear channel assessment process, known as medium sensing, for CSMA, also defining metrics to gauge its effectiveness. In our analysis of CSMA, radar units that detect the medium in use delay their transmission, while those that detect it available can immediately initiate transmission. Our study of CSMA reveals that it outperforms ALOHA across all measured throughputs, yet neither system excels over the other in terms of medium access efficiency.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our cycle-aware
time-encoding is a data-driven method that is rooted in human intuition about
time cycles and enables the discovery of implicit time patterns. Our research
demonstrates enhanced performance on timing prediction tasks by prioritizing time
cycle awareness and employs the low-rank factorization model as a universal
foundation for graph completions, ultimately achieving superior results on multiple
benchmarks in temporal knowledge graph completion.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states like $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, the model must balance the production of authentic and coherent sentences with the generation of new linguistic structures. To achieve this, we introduce SparseGAN, a novel GAN-based text generation model that generates novel sentence structures while maintaining linguistic consistency. Specifically, the generator produces sentences with infrequent OOV (out-of-vocabulary) words, while the discriminator focuses on detecting either the presence of OOV words or the generation of new sentences. To overcome the training difficulties, we employ a sparse cross-entropy loss function that minimizes the reliance on OOV words and enables the generation of sentence structures with an increased vocabulary. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that SparseGAN outperforms other GAN-based text generation models on the Standard Word-Level metrics in multiple languages.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains in finding evidence to support this theory. To tackle this issue, we need to shift from purely philosophical discussions to a more quantitative approach, considering factors such as the survival of microorganisms during long interstellar journeys and the likelihood of detecting them as they travel. Using a computational model, we explored the possibilities of identifying biomarkers of life, such as gas or magnetic fields, in situations where panspermia could occur, and we examined the constraints imposed by the requirements for life to thrive. Our analysis reveals that even over millions of years, the signals of life traveling through space remain extremely faint compared to the intense radiations and radiative fluxes these microorganisms are exposed to. As a result, we found that the most promising environments for detecting life on the move are rare astronomical events with long duration periods, such as gamma-burst protracted deaths or supermassive black hole mergers with low accretion rates, particularly if the associated microorganisms possess advanced magnetic fields to protect themselves.

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using mildly non-linear scales from data that will be obtained from interferometric HI intensity mapping experiments. Assuming that the experiments will be like CHORD and PUMA, we run a series of analyses on mock data that accurately represents how these surveys are conducted at redshift z=0.5, comparing these to the performance that can be expected from stage 4 optical galaxy surveys. The impact of removing foregrounds using methods that rely on simulations is accounted for in the analysis, which shows how it affects the accuracy of the parameter estimation. The 10 parameters that we vary during the analysis consist of 3 cosmological and 7 non-cosmological parameters. The 4 most relevant parameters are the cold dark matter density, the Hubble constant, the primordial power spectrum amplitude and the linear HI bias. When assuming that foregrounds can be effectively removed, our best case scenario finds that the estimated parameters are accurate with less than a 3% error. When including the impact of foregrounds however, all parameters are estimated inaccurately by more than 5 sigma, indicating that foregrounds removal has to be more accurately handled to avoid biases. Scale cuts, specifically a minimum k-value of about 0.03 h/Mpc, need to be imposed in order to get an accurate estimation of the two

The proposed concept of induced spontaneous symmetry breaking is explored through a theoretical scenario. This scenario posits that spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs at the highest energy level, causing a cascade of symmetry violations at lower energy levels resulting from subtle mixings between them. A simple model has been devised to illustrate this idea using scalar portals, where the significant difference in energy scales, such as the Planck and electroweak scales, arises from the multiplication of several small factors related to the mixings. The formation of dark matter fields is also examined in this framework, where it is possible for these fields to emerge from matter fields located on one or more intermediate energy levels between the highest and lowest.

Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.

In designing minimum power networks, we are given an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ along with associated edge costs. The objective is to select an edge subset $F \subseteq E$ satisfying a specific minimum power criterion. Specifically, for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem, F must contain exactly k disjoint st-paths. Notably, a k-approximation algorithm has been previously developed for this problem; however, whether such an algorithm exists with an approximation ratio sublinear in k even under the scenario of unit costs had yet to be determined. We present a new $4\sqrt{2k}$-approximation algorithm applicable to general cost settings.

This study proposes a technique for the autonomous planning of swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles within a predefined environment. When the swarm detects changes, such as the movement of a target, within a designated area, the command center recalculates and adjusts the swarm's flight path. Key algorithms employed in this research are A* pathfinding and Generalized Labeled Multi-Bernoulli for target tracking.

The concept of localization in physics is significant in understanding dynamic processes on complex networks, particularly near critical transitions. This study tackles this issue by measuring nodal activity to quantify localization in networks undergoing dynamic changes. The proposed method is widely applicable and can be employed with theoretical models, simulated data, and real-world observations. The researchers analyze spreading processes on various networks, demonstrating that nodal activity can display intricate patterns depending on the network's architecture. The findings indicate that localized and widespread patterns are not mutually exclusive features in a spreading process. Additionally, the prevalence of an epidemic near a critical transition is influenced by the delocalized component of the network. Furthermore, different critical exponents can coexist with similar localization patterns. The study also reveals a more intricate behavior in quenched networks, influenced by the type of activation and degree exponent. The work sets the stage for future investigations of localized activity in network processes.

Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports can be complicated due to limited access to game data. Previous research developed methods for assessing defensive teams, but these methods didn't account for uncertainty and used all available data equally. Our study developed a valuation method for defensive teams that takes into consideration the probability of successful attacks, which we applied to football data from the UEFA EURO 2020 and 2022 tournaments. We assessed the uncertainty surrounding each team's defensive performance and investigated factors that influence successful attacks, finding that uncertainty has an clear impact, while other variables' effects are less pronounced. Our analysis provided detailed insights into each team's defensive strengths and weaknesses, which we visualized through various diagrams. Furthermore, we investigated factors that influence the probability of successful attacks, including upcoming matches, recent performance, and home and away games, which we found to have a significant impact. Our method is relevant to any sport with clearly definable scoring actions and validated metrics, such as basketball's 'three-point shot' or American football's 'touchdown'.

Extracting information from images of forms is a complex task due to varying layout designs. This complexity increases with old forms that have deteriorated and are contaminated with noise. One crucial step in the extraction process involves linking input text to predefined label fields. Our research offers an innovative, layout-agnostic method for parsing forms by first detecting text on the form and a corresponding target area. We utilize a detection system that locates all text on the form in one operation rather than detecting each text segment individually. Our technique excels in simplicity, efficiency, and effectiveness despite handling difficult layout designs. Our model achieves exceptional results on the IIIT 5000 dataset and significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art by 11.50% in terms of overall accuracy.

Highly flexible recurrent state-space models can capture complex patterns in time series data, but typically assume a static and unchanging dynamic, a rare occurrence in real-world situations. To overcome this limitation, many systems exhibit patterns that are similar yet distinct, and can be described through a single underlying variable. To tackle such scenarios, we developed the Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a novel framework that uses a compact set of latent factors to model interconnected dynamical systems. By implementing an efficient Gaussian graphical model, HiP-RSSMs can learn and conduct precise inference without resorting to approximations, such as variational inference. In our experiments, HiP-RSSMs consistently surpassed traditional state-space models and multi-task competitors on multiple demanding robotic tasks, in both real-world applications and simulations.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We've also identified new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. Moreover, we show that the BBP phase transition in an additive rank-one perturbation of a GUE matrix is a consequence of asymptotic conditional freeness. This line of reasoning applies as well to an analysis of outlier eigenvalues in various unitarily invariant ensembles.

We take a degree-2 cover of a genus-1 curve D over a non-hyperelliptic genus-3 curve C, in a field of characteristic not 2. We construct a genus-2 curve X, such that its Jacobian is connected to a product of the Jacobian of D and X's Jacobian, the Jacobian of C being an isogeny.

Determining the extent of polarization within social systems is vital to studying its effects on political structures. While numerous methods are employed to analyze polarization in social networks through structural evaluation, our analysis revealed that eight commonly used methods yield elevated polarization scores even in artificially constructed networks that closely mirror real-world networks in density and distribution. Furthermore, some of these methods proved sensitive to specific characteristics of polarized groups, such as degree distribution and size. We proposed introducing a standard normalization to mitigate these issues, alongside a comprehensive set of criteria for effective measurement of structural polarization. By normalizing the scores, the classification performance increased by up to 220%, and notably, the choice of measurement method became significantly less crucial, with most methods surpassing the previous best performance following normalization. Our research lays the groundwork for a thorough evaluation and comparison of different structural polarization measurement methods.

The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains analytical tractability. As a result, we can determine the stability of the synchronized state in multilayer networks and design a method for calculating the eigenvalues of a large Jacobian matrix, even if the network has non-zero degree. Furthermore, our approach enables the derivation of explicit conditions for Kuramoto stability in multilayer networks, including a specific condition that arises when the inter-layer connections are weak, in which case the oscillators' frequencies become decoupled, allowing for a more in-depth analysis of each frequency.

Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions involves identifying those relationships that yield a well-defined differential operator. This process is already explored in the context of linear differential operators acting on scalar fields or vector fields. However, the compatibility conditions for a linear differential operator acting on second-order tensor fields, specifically the Cauchy stress operator, are not as well understood. In this work, we provide the complete and most general form of the compatibility conditions for the Cauchy stress operator, using the Lami theorem to simplify them further. Additionally, we investigate the minimal parameterization required to define the stress operator and its conjugate. This research has significant implications for the theory of linear elasticity, given that the approach can be applied to non-symmetric elasticity models and the possibility of relaxing the invertibility condition of the elasticity tensor.

The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue.

We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-based generation. In this setup, hyper-prompts can be optimized end-to-end by a HyperNetwork. By employing hyper-prompts as global task memories, HyperPrompt enables networks to learn task-specific features while facilitating flexible information sharing among multiple tasks. Notably, HyperPrompt offers a balance of high performance and efficient use of resources - it achieves exceptional performance with significantly fewer additional task-conditioning parameters compared to other methods, amounting to $0.14\%$ of the parameters required, ultimately showcasing great computational efficiency. Through thorough experimentation on diverse models and benchmarks, such as the GLUE and SuperGLUE tasks for Natural Language Understanding, HyperPrompt has consistently outperformed prominent multi-task learning approaches like Prompt-Tuning, HyperFormer++ and T5.

Let $\Phi$ be a root system belonging to type $A_l$ or $D_l$. Let $K$ be a field whose characteristic is not $2$. Let $\delta$ be the maximal root in the root system $\Phi$ and define the set $\Phi_0$ as consisting of the roots $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ for which $\alpha$ is orthogonal to $\delta$. The group $G_{\text{sc}}(\alpha)$ is then determined as a subgroup of a specific semisimple group over the field $K$. When $\Phi$ is of type $A_l$, it is shown that the set $\Phi_0$ contains $l-1$ elements and when $\Phi$ is of type $D_l$, it is shown that the set $\Phi_0$ contains $d-1$ elements, where $d$ is the number of columns in a specific arrangement configuration. Vectors associated with roots in the set $\Phi_0$ are shown to be equidistributed under certain conjugation operations within a specific irreducible representation of a Chevalley group. This equidistribution does not hold for vectors associated with the root $\delta$.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, the system only emits photons in 2$n$ correlations, and this emission's purity is improved by the parity symmetry, mainly due to reduced odd-correlated photon emissions. The parity symmetry of the system can be controlled and adjusted with a magnetic field to switch between even and odd correlated photons. This research advances the study of photon bundle emission in the ultrastrong coupling regime and enables the exploration of protected multi-quanta phenomena.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node.

Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the nonparametric method match
queue length data from probe vehicles, offering a promising alternative for
traffic state estimation.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds.

The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by LHCb, at centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV and an accumulated luminosity of 3 $fb^{-1}$, yields 4 standard deviation excess beyond predicted background counts with no noticeable features found in dimuon invariant mass spectra.

Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform.

This lecture will provide an elementary overview of both transverse and longitudinal beam dynamics, in addition to key beam loss phenomena in circular accelerators, catering to attendees with minimal to no prior understanding of this topic.

Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II, incorporating features like easy user interface, modular code, and integratable robotics for enhanced efficiency and productivity in experiments.

We have derived improved differentiability properties for solutions to a non-autonomous obstacle problem, formulated as
  \begin{equation*}
  \min \left\{\int_{\Omega}f\left(x, Dv(x)\right)dx\,:\, v\in
  \mathcal{K}_\psi(\Omega)\right\}.
  \end{equation*} Given the growth restrictions imposed on the function $f$, with respect to the gradient variable, we find that when the obstacle function is bounded and satisfies certain regularity conditions, the partial map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ being part of the Sobolev space, leads to a corresponding increase in the differentiability of the solution, provided the partial map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ belongs to a $W^{1, p+2}$. Notably, we address subquadratic growth conditions on the function $f$, i.e., where $f(x,\xi)\approx a(x)|\xi|^p$ and $1<p<2$ and map $a$ also belongs to a Sobolev space, where $\Omega$ and $x,\xi\in \Omega$.

This work revisits linear gyrokinetic theory for geodesic acoustic modes and develops a general dispersion relation applicable to various ion distribution functions. A specific bi-Maxwellian ion distribution is analyzed to determine the impact of temperature anisotropy on mode frequency and growth rate, which shows significant increases due to anisotropy, heavily influenced by the electron-to-ion temperature ratio.

A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves gradually transforming an initial Hamiltonian representing easy-to-solve problems into a target Hamiltonian representing the problems to be solved, and then determining the problem's solution by examining the optimized ground state of the interpolated Hamiltonian. Quantum annealing's effectiveness relies on the interplay between quantum fluctuations and classical spins; however, this process can fail if the interpolated Hamiltonian causes sudden parallax shifts during the annealing process, paralyzing the quantum computer. To address this issue, the parameter $\lambda$ in the quantum annealing algorithm needs to be reduced below a certain threshold that depends on the strength of the quantum fluctuations and decoherence. Decoherence, which represents the influence of the environment on the quantum system, can also hinder the failure by the quantum annealing algorithm, and it is shown that decoherence allows the algorithm to succeed even if the Hamiltonian is non-stoquastic.

This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study.

We provide a detailed explanation for a part of Serre's conjecture related to GL_2 through Kummer theory, thereby bypassing the reliance on p-adic Hodge theory. This involves utilizing descriptions of crystalline extension reductions, Kummer theory, Abrashkin's findings, local class field theory, Dembele-Diamond-Roberts' earlier work, Brueckner-Shaferevich-Vostokov's reciprocity laws and their implications to describe and calculate certain G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles.

We establish a precise result for optimal solutions in an isoperimetric problem outside a confined object within the scenario where a large amount of volume is considered on the mesoscale. This achievement comes from a previously unknown property, termed'mesoscale flatness,' that is shown to be a reliable, if not necessary, condition for solutions in a specific class of surface scenarios with bounded mean curvature. A key aspect of our finding is the validation of a specific version of the mesoscale flatness condition for surfaces with bounded mean curvature that is broader than earlier proven results for surfaces with negative curvature. Another important aspect is the application of a surface variation method, along with a key lemma regarding surface area evolution that enables the recovery of monotonicity results. Additionally, we demonstrate that a specific version of the mesoscale flatness condition is capable of being violated at a minimal scale for surface scenarios with bounded mean curvature.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying the critic networks to them, the method significantly reduces the communication overhead associated with batch updates. During training, the local networks are repeatedly optimized to minimize the difference between their updated outputs and the original network's outputs, effectively reducing errors and facilitating efficient convergence. Our research demonstrates that this method yields a substantial decrease in training time when utilizing a large dataset, leading to a high performance in image classification tasks.

Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential in improving safety systems.  Due to their intrinsic properties, these materials can detect deformations and damage, supplementing their sensing capabilities with durability.  However, the high complexity of the material's impedance spectrum hinders the effective detection of damage using conventional sensors.  A novel approach is proposed to enhance the sensitivity of self-sensing composite materials by incorporating a genetic algorithm in electrical impedance spectroscopy.  This method first image-reconstructs the spatial impedance distribution within the material using tomographic reconstruction from a limited set of measurement frequencies.  Secondly, the algorithm accurately identifies the time when damage occurs and its precise spatial extent by optimizing the difference between simulated and actual impedance spectra.  The efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated through numerical simulations and experimental verification under static loading conditions.  The results show that the genetic algorithm efficiently pinpoints the damage location and extent in self-sensing composite materials.  The proposed technique has the potential to accurately detect cracks in composite materials, enabling the development of damage-shaping capabilities through active feedback control, thus enhancing their reliability in critical applications.

We're exploring the possibility that there's a parallel between brain neurons and societal individuals, inquiring whether collective intelligence requires individual intellect and what specific forms of individual knowledge contribute to greater collective insight. By integrating principles from connectionism, agent-based modeling, group psychology, economics, and physics, we reframe these concepts through the lens of changing system dynamics. Ultimately, we apply this understanding to explain the coexistence of prey and predator species in the Lotka-Volterra model and the catastrophic consequences of particular individual intellect applications.

We have designed a control method using learning algorithms to manage complex systems based on limited and imperfect observations of their behavior. This algorithm excels in multiple settings, such as environments with multiple degrees of freedom, dynamic systems and those that respond differently to various inputs, even with a lack of specific information about their structure. It achieves remarkable results when faced with unfamiliar dynamics in just one trial, using a combination of simple models that capture the relationships between the system's inputs and outputs. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a variety of dynamic systems, including a quadcopter, a swimmer with flexible limbs and a humanoid robot, among others. It successfully controlled these systems within a single trial, using side information about their design.

This work proposes a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces centered on geometric vector techniques and illustrates the method's efficacy through a variety of vector integrand identities proved using this framework.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs is considered within a certain "duration" window where the mass difference between two lepton types lies between their sum and the absolute difference. Although a moderately large interaction between this scalar field and the two lepton types could lead to extended lifetimes and larger observable distances between their birth and death points, the condition that this scalar's self-coupling must be very small limits its potential for such behavior. As a result, its primary characteristic is a short, typically sub-millimeter, mean free path. Despite this, it has the potential to significantly impact muon g-2 and Higgs decay into muons, and could also be detected through rare muon decay events.

This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Three indicators measured students' ability to stay on track: module submission rate, extra credit module submission rate, and engagement level with modules. Four demographic variables were analyzed - Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status, and First-generation status - and students were categorized into two groups based on each variable. Comparative analyses between the demographics within each variable were conducted to identify the effect of remote learning on student engagement and performance. Statistical significance was determined using the independent samples test. Findings showed that remote learning had a negative impact on submission rates and engagement levels for some demographics, no impact on others, and even a positive impact on submission rates for a few. The research highlights the heterogeneity in the impact of remote learning on university students' ability to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course.

All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent by a Lie algebra based path integral formulation. This document is intended to outline the means through which this higher level of symmetry is exhibited within a specific subset of Toda conformal field theories, particularly those associated with the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ algebra. A particular set of Ward identities, which are inherently linked to the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ algebra and its associated degenerate representations, are identified and their direct derivation is demonstrated. Furthermore, this document demonstrates the interconnection between these identities and the spin-three correlation function, which is itself a fundamental aspect of the theory. A distinct set of quadratic identities is shown to systematically yield the spin-three correlation function when subjected to a specific transformation. This transformation is, in turn, defined by the Fock-Zamolodchikov equation, which is itself a derivative of the Ward identity.
We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, verifying that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory for near-extremal black holes is confirmed by observing that scalar field scattering does not cause a transition from a regular singularity to a singular one. However, the theory fails for extremal black holes, as their nature does not depend on the scattering of a particular energy but rather their initial extremality.

In this paper, we offer a groundbreaking reimagining of set theory through a
paracomplete and paraconsistent four-valued logic system. Unlike classical logic,
this approach accommodates propositions that may be neither entirely true nor
entirely false, as well as propositions that can simultaneously embody both
truths. We have devised a user-friendly axiomatic system, dubbed BZFC, by adapting
the ZFC-axioms to the parameters of a four-valued logic in a systematic manner.
Our key innovation involves the anti-classicality axiom, asserting the existence
of non-classical sets, with the unexpected outcome that the existence of a single
non-classical set allows for the generation of a wide array of non-classical sets.
Furthermore, our analysis encompasses the relationship between our proposed system
BZFC and classical ZFC, demonstrating that the two logics exhibit bidirectional
interpretability. We also demonstrate an interesting application concerning Tarski
semantics by showing how the traditional definition of the satisfaction relation
faithfully represents the non-classical properties inherent in our proposed system
BZFC.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions.

If a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree that is not a line has a non-trivial action, we prove that its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree.

In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our proposed model, a deep long-short-term memory-based approach, simultaneously detects and model temporal changes in directed connectivity between brain regions, leveraging multivariate time series data, ultimately demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in tasks that assess connectivity changes.

Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate accurate phylogeny reconstruction, various stochastic processes have been developed to generate random phylogenetic trees or networks, which can be used to validate results or inform Bayesian analysis. Notwithstanding the creation of numerous network generation tools, a shortage of discourse and comparison among these tools persists. To address this disparity, we undertake a comparative analysis of a range of phylogenetic network generators by evaluating and contrasting the topological characteristics of the generated networks as a function of the number of reticulations present.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns.

The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, obtained through direct inversion. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN achieves a faster convergence rate than the Neumann Series, with an optimal parameter value that scales linearly with the iteration number. Furthermore, we derive an iterative formula for the variance of the estimated inverse, which enables the optimization of NN through the use of score functions. The distinctive feature of NN, which uses an iterative rather than a static preconditioning matrix, invites comparison with the Newton iteration. Through the substitution of a specific matrix, we demonstrate that NN can be viewed as a higher-order version of the Newton iteration. Consequently, we propose a new method, titled 'Nested Newton' (NNN), which applies this matrix substitution directly, resulting in a method with a convergence rate one order higher than NN. The resulting NNN algorithm represents a general higher-order iteration method for matrix inversion, which can be used for data with non-Gaussian distribution.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and correlations arising from the scattering matrix, including constraints on the internal energy distribution that must be met for any incident wave pattern, and reveals that certain sums of specific eigenchannel probabilities equal the fraction of system energy lost due to absorption. Additionally, the inherent symmetry of the scattering matrix generates constrained correlations between different eigenchannels, and particular relationships exist between the fractions of system energy lost in different channels, or between different channels and the total lost energy. These constraints apply universally to any scattering system and are demonstrated to create opportunities for enhancing energy deposition in representative examples.

We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also revealing that the topological amplitude displays long-range correlations with the disorder strength. Additionally, we show that the topological amplitude can be probed experimentally using the response of the system to a small binary disorder.

This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. Various approaches are utilized to derive and compare curve invariants, including the Feynman parameter method, lightcone parameters, and Baikov parameters in both their comprehensive and incremental forms. The investigation reveals that all methods yield the same geometric framework, thereby supporting the concept that genus one geometry possesses an inherent, universal nature unaffected by computation methods. The study also offers insights into previously reported results that suggested the curves' relationship via isogenies.

This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the gluon fusion with the decay channel $pp \to \phi b\bar{b}$, with $\phi$ representing a neutral Higgs boson. The discussion includes the influence of complex parameters on the on-shell width and the CP-odd component of the light Higgs boson, with a related study on the detection of the light Higgs boson in the $b\bar{b}$ channel via on-shell production

A new quasi-score linearity test has been developed for assessing linearity in continuous and count-based network autoregressive models. The test's asymptotic distribution is analyzed under various scenarios, including fixed and increasing network dimensions, null hypotheses, and specific alternative hypotheses. Key findings indicate that when model parameters are identifiable, the test's distribution converges to the chi-square and noncentral chi-square forms. Notably, the results are robust to parameters at their space boundaries. For non-identifiable parameters, an alternative test has been proposed, along with an established asymptotic distribution for a fixed network dimension.
