The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many decades. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos as they offer a direct and magnetically unbiased glimpse into hadronic interactions of cosmic rays. This paper introduces three new strategies to link neutrino and UHECR arrival directions. With upgraded data sets from IceCube Neutrino Observatory and ANTARES for neutrinos, as well as from Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array for UHECRs, statistical significance and accuracy are significantly enhanced. The analyses comprise searching for UHECR-UHECR spatial correlations around neutrino sources, searching for neutrinos accompanied by UHECR sources, and neutrino-UHECR spatial correlations within compact systems. None of these analyses uncovered a notable correlation above $3\sigma$. Consequently, we present upper limits on the neutrino-UHECR correlation function, making it feasible to constrain source models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that numerous models can be ruled out with the current data sets, and future experiments like the upgraded IceCube and KM3NeT will be capable of investigating a broader range of source scenarios.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for handling the outlier class and metadata were found to yield superior results.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal force, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restorative forces, thus dictating the size of the developed finger. Numerical computation techniques are utilized to analyze not just nonlinear finger patterns but also modes with both circumferentially confined folds and branches that occur with variations in the rate of rotation and imposed pressure. Bifurcation diagrams representing a variety of states, including both reflection-symmetric states and asymmetric states, are presented in this study. The relationship between the size of the membrane system and a particular nonlinear state is shown to influence the structure of the banded solution that emerges with increased tension. The size of the system is found to impact the number of inner fluid pockets that form on the outer fluid when multiple-electrode projections are utilized.

Microscopic dynamics can be analyzed using nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, Michael Kugler's thesis explores this connection by developing a method for determining nonequilibrium currents directly from microscopic dynamics. Currents are calculated using a specific microcanonical distribution of Hamiltonian trajectories, this approach avoids volume changes in phase space which occur during expansions. To test this method, it was applied to the expansion of a one-dimensional hard-point gas where the initial conditions were set to represent a nonequilibrium state. Observed results showed that the calculated stationary currents compared favorably to those obtained from the stationary Boltzmann distribution. Additionally, the calculated stationary densities compared favorably to theoretical predictions made by the Boltzmann equation for a specific scenario where the collision rate is high.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. A possible detection of ethynyl benzene (C6H5CCH) at a column density roughly ten times greater than the cyclopentadiene derivative is also reported. The calculated abundances for cyano derivatives of cyclopentadiene and benzene are notably lower than previously recorded figures. The ethynyl and cyano derivatives of the cyclical compounds possess a rotational temperature very close to the cloud's kinetic temperature. The relative abundance of the ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers was found to be roughly 1.4 times greater than the abundance of the two cyano cyclopentadiene isomers, which may reflect the abundance of the parent radicals CCH and CN. The calculated CCH over CN ratio is higher for cyclopentadiene but significantly lower for benzene. The formation of the cyclical compounds in TMC-1 can be attributed to a reaction pathway based on neutral-neutral reactions, which also suggests benzene's expected abundance should be comparable to that of cyclopentadiene.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that directly assesses relationships between target words. The proposed mechanism is easily integrated into state-of-the-art attention-based neural machine translation models, leading to significant improvements in translation accuracy and natural language coherence, particularly in cases where the model is tasked with generating long target sentences.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on application translation. Nonetheless, despite achieving success with a translational approach, the development of grid services remained incomplete, leading to the necessity for an alternate methodology, namely reverse translation.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its quintessence-like nature, it surpasses the phantom barrier. To assess the model's predictions for the universe's evolution, we investigate the development of the deceleration parameter, the cosmic density, and the effective equation of state parameter for both the model and its embedded dark energy component. Our findings also support a value of 8 × 10^6 Pa.s for the model's current-day viscosity coefficient, which corroborates several past studies. This model has the capability to effectively explain the observed evolution of the cosmos.

In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  Our proposed system is designed to address this need by incorporating an evolutionary algorithm and a neural network to model two aspects of curiosity: intrinsic and extrinsic motivation.  Based on observations of students in a science learning environment, our results show that the system accurately identifies curiosity in real-time, capturing the complex interactions between motivation, curiosity, and academic achievement.  By providing data on (1) curiosity levels, (2) learning content, and (3) motivation, our system can facilitate teacher-student knowledge sharing, provide personalized recommendations for increasing curiosity and learning effectiveness, and enable empirical validation of educational theories.  Specifically, the system enables empirical validation of the Self-Determination Theory by demonstrating the five-digit profile of autonomy, competence, relatedness, intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, and curiosity levels before, during, and after the learning process.  Furthermore, the system highlights the significance of curiosity in bridge-building between the sender and receiver of learning content, and highlights the need for future research on the dynamics of curiosity in group learning.

Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly more limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research presents an unbiased Gaussian process model tailored to undirected graphs, which draws inspiration from Mat\'ern smoothness properties commonly employed in the Euclidean space.  By leveraging the stochastic partial differential equations that characterize Mat\'ern Gaussian fields in the Euclidean space, the researchers develop a novel Gaussian process model capable of capturing Mat\'ern smoothness properties within the context of undirected graphs.  In addition, they investigate the conditions under which this model is compatible with Bayesian inference, and provide an analytical expression for the marginal log-likelihood function. Furthermore, this research involves an investigation of model asymptotic behavior, a specific example of model application, and an examination of its computational efficiency.

The effective management of urban roads plays a crucial role in the optimal operation of urban transportation systems and overall city functioning. Current monitoring techniques rely heavily on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourced data, but they often come with limitations of high costs, restricted coverage areas, or unreliable data due to low user participation rates. In this study, a groundbreaking approach of mobile sensing is presented, utilizing a large fleet of ridesharing vehicles to monitor and interpret the condition of urban roads as they traverse through the network. Our analysis assesses the sensing performance of this approach based on several key factors including road segments covered, data collection frequency, signal noise, and measurement errors. Our goal is to minimize the variance of mobile sensors' readings while ensuring the road network remains connected. This optimization problem is solved through a robust filter algorithm, taking into account real-world data collected from over 150,000 trips in New York City. Our results show that a relatively small number of ridesharing vehicles are needed to provide accurate measurements of urban road conditions, and that a network with high connectivity can maintain optimal performance even with a significant increase in road segments covered. Furthermore, practical challenges and potential applications of this approach are discussed, along with policy implications for the optimal allocation of city resources.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying neutrino masses and different dark matter formations. These operators cause the hadronic system within J/ψ to break apart, thereby making the decay visible. We calculated the observables for the following processes: J/ψ photoproduction, hadronic invariant mass, and lepton pair masses. Through these observables and a global fit, we derived exclusion limits for each effective field theory operator with various neutrino masses and dark matter formations. These limits were found to be more stringent than existing ones and could be further narrowed by global fits using additional experimental data, particularly for certain operator types.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications involving the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Yet, surprisingly, little research has focused on comprehending the complex workings of these algorithms, particularly those that operate behind closed doors. Previous studies revealed the ease with which these scoring models can be manipulated. This paper aims to investigate the underlying causes of this unexpected sensitivity and instability. By employing the latest advances in interpretation, we examined the relative importance of essay features, including coherence, relevance, vocabulary, and content in influencing automated scores. We used this to investigate the issues of over-sensitivity (small changes yielding significantly varying output scores) and over-stability (little change in scores resulting from significant changes in input) associated with these scoring models. The findings indicated that although autoscoring models are trained with the ability to process complex contextual information (similar to BERT-based models), they instead behave like simpler bag-of-words models that are overly reliant on isolated key phrases. As a result, these models are prone to both over-sensitivity and over-stability. We proposed several defenses to enhance the robustness of autoscoring models, including the incorporation of peer review and human evaluation of candidate responses in addition to the scores output by these models.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,b)/2}$ holds, where $p(t,x)$ is the probability that, during the interval $[1,t]$, the random walk $S$ with zero-mean increments has spent a fraction of time greater than $x$ with non-negative values, occurring for a random walk with the parameter $b$ (related to the L\'evy parameter $\alpha$ as $b=\alpha^{-1}$) with an exponential decay rate $\phi(x,b)$, for which the value at $x=0.5$ is $\frac{1.77}{\sqrt{\log t}}$. This probability $p(t,x)$ displays the following behavior for specific values of $x$: for $x$ close to $1$, the decay rate $\phi(x,b)$ is $\frac{1.77}{\sqrt{\log t}}$; for $x$ close to $0$, the probability $p(t,x)$ remains constant over time, with a value of $\frac{1}{2}$; for $x$ in between $0$ and $1$, the probability $p(t,x)$ exhibits non-monotonic behavior with respect to $x$ and the parameter $b$.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source achieves the desired helicon mode of discharge, which relies on sensitive measurements and requires careful consideration of device interconnections. A new study involving UHF probe diagnostics has confirmed that the plasma source enters the helicon mode, and has provided the necessary parameters to operate it effectively. The findings indicate that a high-density plasma with a temperature of around 5 eV and 1.4 Pa m of impeadance is achievable when using a 13.56 MHz frequency and 3000 W of power.

In comparison to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial pesticides exhibit numerous advantages, which can be modelled through a system where entomopathogenic nematodes are used to eliminate and concurrently suppress the population of target insects. This system aims to manage pests through a continuous nematode release mechanism, where the model's equilibrium and Hopf bifurcation periodic solutions are analyzed for optimal pest control, which is further confirmed by numerical simulations and case studies.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like marking abnormal cells in histopathology images. To streamline this process, a semi-automatic system for detecting and exacting markers from histopathology images would be very useful. However, building such a system is complicated due to the presence of irregularly shaped backgrounds, varying illumination, and overlapping structures in these images. In this paper, we focus on developing a system for detecting and outlining cell nuclei in histopathology images. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel detection-extraction network called W-Net, which treats detection and extraction as two interconnected tasks. Specifically, we design an extension of the U-Net called D-Net to detect the center of the object, and integrate this with W-Net to guide the network to extract the object based on the detected center. To train the network, we use synthetic data generated by superimposing nuclei on histopathology images, which are then annotated automatically using the detected centers. Our experiments show that the proposed system is highly accurate, achieving an AUC of 0.94 for detecting and an MSE of 103.90 for extracting nuclei on a test dataset of 1000 images.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2r+1)(F) or Sp(2r)(F) respectively. In this setting, we've obtained a key conclusion in our study - the converse theorem for G applies locally, allowing the determination of a given irreducible automorphic representation of G through its restriction to a product of GL(1) and explicit computations. This outcome holds particularly true when F has a quadratic extension, in which case we can further identify the representation using Chebotarev's density theorem after a suitable passage of induction. Our approach in this study involves utilizing the local converse theorem to explore the representation π in a scenario where its L-function L(s, π) exhibits a specified behavior following a change of variables, allowing us to recover the Femeri's theorem on non-implementability of certain Galois extensions through Finiteness theorem. Moreover, we establish the converse theorem for G by linking the automorphic representation π to the given data of density, and this result is in line with the work of Langlands in his 1969 paper 'Problems in the theory of Gel'fand.

Xiong and Liu previously provided a definition for graphs G that have hamiltonian n-th iterated line graphs, L^n(G), where n is 2 or greater. In this study, we examine whether an L^n(G) graph possesses a hamiltonian path, and offer a definition for G to achieve this condition. Additionally, we apply this definition to set multiple upper limits for a graph's hamiltonian path index.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory interventions, shifting cell death from pyroptotic to a less inflammatory form, like apoptosis. Furthermore, we are integrating this single-cell model into the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator, as part of a multidisciplinary coalition focused on understanding COVID-19's host-dynamics, to gain deeper insight into the effects of pyroptosis at a cellular level.

External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by introducing unanticipated fluctuations in the reward signal. This concept is mathematically formalized, and the conditions are identified under which an environment involving uncontrollable state variables can be broken down into two separate components: an environment solely affected by the uncontrollable state and reward variables, and an environment defined by the variables that can be controlled. Additionally, a condition for reducing the complexity of these variables in Monte Carlo policy evaluation is established, leading to potential acceleration of this process. This acceleration could be applied across a broader range of reinforcement learning algorithms. Two methods are devised for identifying the uncontrollable state variables, and the results from applying these methods to multiple test environments show a notable increase in efficiency and a potential for speeding up the reinforcement learning process.

A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is generating high demands for static verification. To fulfill this need, our project HELMHOLTZ is introduced in this article as a static verification tool specifically designed for Michelson, a statically-typed programming language used in the Tezos blockchain. By integrating Michelson with a user-defined specification through refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accurately checks the correctness of a Michelson program. As the basis of this project, a type system for refinement types in Michelson is defined along with a static verification algorithm that leverages abstraction functions to ensure the correctness of Michelson programs. To enhance usability, a user-friendly interface and multiple examples are also provided to demonstrate the capabilities of HELMHOLTZ.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a specific characteristic, using a Chern-Simons action modified by the addition of a specific term. This modification yields black holes and solitons with properties that are influenced by a complex scalar field and are also affected by conserved quantities such as electric charge and isospin. The added term causes a non-linear relationship between the scalar field and the gravitational field. This relationship results in the formation of solitons with stable properties, as well as rotating black holes with hair that is influenced by the gravitational field. This transformation allows the use of the Chern-Simons formalism to describe charged black holes and solitons within this modified gravity theory. The solitons can also be described using a non-linear interconnection between the scalar field and the gravitational field, which allows the derivation of their static properties. The addition of a magnetic field to the solitons causes a splitting of the isospin coefficients, leading to the separation of isospin charges. This separation enables the existence of objects with charges that are composed of multiple isospin units.

Theories of supersymmetric Yang-Mills with algebra so(4N) can have non-trivial, invertible-defying symmetries. By utilizing holographic duality, we can determine the branes equivalent to these symmetries, and deduce the fusion principles for the symmetries through brane dynamics.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning.

The concept of Boolean Ramsey numbers for sets of posets was initially explored in relation to Boolean lattices and posets obtained from chains with minimal elements combined into a V-shaped structure. A key objective is to establish a minimum number 'n' for any number of color options where a given V-shaped poset will be entirely colored with a specific color in a Boolean lattice. Recent work has led to the determination of Boolean Ramsey numbers for specific instances, and this paper aims to build on that by investigating the same concept for V-shaped posets and identifying minimum posets containing the Ramsey property in Boolean lattices of a particular size. Another area of research within this paper focuses on Boolean rainbow Ramsey numbers which involve identifying whether a particular structure within a Boolean lattice is monochromatic given 'n' color options. This study explores this concept for V-shaped posets and their antichains.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds. Our approach divides the grid into sub-regions and applies dynamic programming within each sub-region, treating boundaries as absorbing states. We then use the values obtained from intra-regional calculations to guide inter-regional interactions, ensuring that our hierarchical solution approximates the optimal value of the original problem. Our method facilitates the exploration of how scale affects game outcomes and yields computationally efficient results, with significant reductions in both memory and processing requirements compared to a flat policy.

Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the unit cube is designated as 'cyclic' if it satisfies a specific inequality relating its components and the uniform distribution. The term 'nontransitive' is applied to an n-tuple '(x_1, \ldots, x_n)' if for every index i, the probability of the event '(x_i, x_{i+1})' exceeds the probability of the event '(x_{i+1}, x_i)'. Nontransitive n-tuples are shown to occupy a measureable portion of the unit cube by employing an inductive method. Furthermore, the set of cyclic n-tuples is demonstrated to comprise a substantial segment of the unit cube utilizing an inductive approach, and we also establish that the limit of the sequence of cyclic n-tuples, as n tends to infinity, corresponds to a specific geometric shape within the unit cube.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the cycleGAN framework can be a limitation, as multiple applications require the generation of diverse images from a single input, such as converting multiple modalities from a single CT scan, generating multiple organs from a single MRI scan, or creating multiple anonymous versions from a single image. To address this issue, the paper introduces a novel adaptive instance normalization switchable cycleGAN, featuring a single unified generator that can produce multiple output images by incorporating the global information of the input data properly. The proposed framework achieves impressive results on the enhancement of low-dose CT images, outperforming the cycleGAN with separate generators by a margin of 1.12 in PSNR and 6.56 in SSIM, according to the evaluation protocol. Furthermore, the method exhibits flexibility in multiple-except-one image-to-image translation tasks, surpassing the state-of-the-art cycleGAN models in visual coherence and realism, with scores of 1.53 and 1.35 respectively. The code for the method is available online.

Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider data structure in the batch dimension and overlook the hierarchical nature of trees. To address this limitation, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model that leverages the information embedded in parse trees. Specifically, SPACE-2 uses a tree-structured contrastive loss function that groups related nodes together and treats them as distinct classes. Through the addition of a memory bank dynamic routing module, the model is able to learn from unlabelled dialog context. Extensive experiments conducted on the Dialog Redo Task and the Dialog LLOD Task demonstrate SPACE-2's effectiveness, with the model achieving notable improvements over the baseline models including BART and T5. The code and model weights for SPACE-2 are publicly available for download.

This research aims to examine the geometric makeup of an ideal fluid's spacetime 
when coupled with a particular vector field and specific potential function. 
We've derived three key non-flat solutions that fit this description, and found 
that under specific conditions, these solutions can be used to describe the 
spacetime surrounding a spherically symmetric static object with mass $m$ and 
charge $\mathcal{Q}$. When the charge is zero, this becomes the familiar 
Rosen metric, while when the fluid's gamma parameter is set to a particular value, 
we find a solution related to the Reissner-Nordstr\"om spacetime.

To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halos, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions derived from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum. Our self-consistent approach effectively accounts for interactions between single particle bound states and the continuum across ground and rotational states. By analyzing rotational states in isotopes of $^{42}$Mg and $^{44}$Mg, specifically excitation energy, configuration, and density distribution, our research demonstrates that deformed halo structures endure from intrinsic ground states to collective rotational states, particularly illustrating shape decoupling effects in rotating distorted halo nuclei.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context, a new framework called the "Effective Vector Boson Approximation" (EVBA) is proposed, allowing the weak bosons to participate directly in scattering processes or serve as external fields influencing incoming leptons. Ultimately, the EVBA is demonstrated to incorporate the effects of weak radiative corrections, leading to more precise predictions for muon-muon and muon-electron scattering that surpass the accuracy of the Standard Model at several TeV. Additionally, the EVBA facilitates the direct detection of the Higgs boson's rare muon-photon decay in muon colliders, a process that involves a $e^+ \gamma$ observable and a $e^+ \mu$ contamination that cannot be disregarded at the Higgs production threshold.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields a
significant improvement in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios.

The paper provides derivations of Li-Yau and Souplet-Zhang type estimates for the equation $u_t=\Delta_\xi p + \lambda u + A(u)$ in a complete, non-compact metric measure space with compact boundary. Furthermore, the paper includes local gradient estimates for the equation $\Delta_\xi(u^p)+\lambda u + A(u) = 0$ on complete, non-compact manifolds with compact boundary.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

When the population is not fully known in advance, sampling occurs in sequence, either individually or in batches, which are obtained sequentially. This work presents a novel algorithm that allows for sequential selection of a balanced sample. The algorithm accommodates equal and unequal inclusion probabilities and can also be applied to select spatially balanced samples when the population contains geographical coordinates. Moreover, an investigation using simulated data reveals that the proposed method surpasses alternative methods.

In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using images is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image. Experimental results using the widely used BOP benchmark and BOP-Vis dataset showed that our approach achieved the lowest average calibration error of 1.12 mm when using the MSRA dataset and 2.32 mm when using the BOP-Vis dataset. Our findings suggest that calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using a single image is feasible with an average error of less than 3 mm, enabling its integration in robotic applications requiring low-level control.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds.

Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz frequency bands for communication. However, signal transmission in these bands is severely impacted by high frequecy loss and limited communication distance. To overcome this limitation, a multi-hop communication approach has been proposed to extend the coverage range. We investigate an interesting problem related to this approach, centered around optimizing beam training in a scenario where the base station and terminal equipment are geospatially distanced. In this setting, we develop a novel model that enables the efficient resolution of a complex optimization issue through reinforcement learning. Our proposed scheme involves a data transfer phase that relies on a look-up-based approach to minimize energy consumption, while the beam training phase is optimized via a Q-learning algorithm. Our simulations demonstrate that our scheme leads to a substantial reduction in energy consumption, with energy savings of up to 75% in certain scenarios.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis.

This research presents a novel annotation and correction tool for Arabic texts,
namely MADARi, catering to Standard and Dialectal varieties. MADARi offers a user-
friendly interface and efficient management capabilities for annotating and handling
a considerable volume of texts. Its key features encompass a range of morphological
annotations, such as identifying the base form of words, associated clitics, part of
speech, lemma, translation, and dialect-specific markers. To facilitate productivity
and cost-effectiveness, MADARi offers a range of cost models and quality control
mechanisms. Furthermore, this project is an expansion of the MADAR corpus initiative
focused on Arabic dialects, and the interface is available at https://madar.tamu.edu/madari/.

Planets similar to Earth, orbiting nearby stars with reduced energy output, are being extensively studied and several are suited for further analysis. Focusing on temperate worlds surrounded by thick H2 atmospheres, our models follow chemical transformations and gas circulation after H2O, H2S, CH4, NH3, and CO2 molecules break down. Weve run simulations on multiple ring systems surrounding these planets with varying ring positions and models predicting atmospheric breakdown produce distinct spectral patterns that change with ring composition and atmospheric interactions. Utilizing the MARS-CCD instrument on the 8.2m VLT equivalent NISP instrument on the JWST, our results show that even with high-orbiting exoplanets, we can collect usable data, offering possibilities to verify our theoretical spectra through observations of temperate worlds surrounded by thick H2 atmospheres.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperatures decrease in proportion to T^(2r-1), with r defined as the exponential product of the resistance and a universal constant divided by the Planck's constant (all values below 1/2), non-Majorana-induced zero-energy peaks fragment into two separate peaks at non-zero temperatures, displaying varying conductance in relation to temperature by way of a power law. Furthermore, tunneling associated with a Majorana mode falls within the same broad class of universal behaviors as does the case for unstable critical points with a non-Majorana mode.

The development of advanced detection algorithms through deep learning has accelerated the identification of road issues, including automatic defect detection and marking analysis. To expedite and reduce costs associated with manual inspections, a comprehensive system called RoadAtlas has been developed, providing a holistic solution encompassing road flaw detection, marking parsing, interactive data visualization through a web interface, and a robust database framework supported by API tools.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH) through a set of properties that demonstrate a close resemblance to the properties defining THH. Within this context, we establish a direct connection between the concept of shadows and the broader theory of traces in bicategories. This connection allows us to derive the fundamental properties of shadows as a natural consequence of the properties of traces. Additionally, we explore how both the category of topological spaces and the category of algebraic theories exhibit the capacity for extension of scalars, which in turn enables the computation of their THH through the application of shadows.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive loss function. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, category, and annotation details, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories with sound sources. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate.

A new method has been created that successfully transfers squeezed states into optical cavities even in stable conditions. The method builds upon conventional optomechanical setups, utilizing a three-level atom to facilitate the transfer. Two techniques were devised to observe the squeezed state transfer effect, including applying a controlled influx of squeezed phonons and simulating the system in an environment of phonon-squeezed vibrations. Our model demonstrates the ability to efficiently achieve this transfer in optomechanical systems.

We examine an expansion of modal $\mu$-calculus, specifically considering its application to sets comprised of fundamental elements and investigate its core properties. The complexity of model verification can be resolved for orbit-finite structures, and a parallel connection with parity games exists. In contrast, the issue of determining satisfaction becomes insoluble. Additionally, the limitations of modal $\mu$-calculi with enriched atoms are identified, and we explore how the expressive potential of these systems depends on both the arrangement of these atoms and whether a basic or composite syntax is employed.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2004 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, the gauge freedom is found to relate to the diffeomorphism group.  This note examines how this gauge freedom ties into the degrees of freedom in massive gravity, specifically in relation to the vDVZ discontinuity and the Kogan-Rubin effect.  It is shown that the harmonic gauge can be implemented in a way that separates the five scalar degrees of freedom associated with the massive graviton into four modes governed by the conformally invariant plane and one mode governed by a mass-dependent potential within the conformally flat plane.  This distinction resolves the discrepancy between the results obtained from applying the harmonic gauge to the linearized gravity in the metric and the gravitational scalar fields.

A signed graph is created by adding a polarity to the edges of an existing graph, and this concept of signed graphs has recently been integrated with other graph theory ideas like minors and coloring. By examining the notion of Extended Double Covers, recently proposed by researchers, this work delves deeper into understanding the relationships between planar signed graphs and their connections to the Four-Color Theorem. The authors present a new conjecture, stating that certain graphs which allow homomorphisms to any planar signed graph, will themselves also be able to receive homomorphisms to any planar signed graph, and then prove a related theorem for a certain subclass of graphs without a K_4 minor, and explore near optimal bounds for other subclasses. Additionally, this work introduces the idea of assigning weights to the polarity of edges in a graph, expanding the definition of a signed graph.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representations and metaplectic operators, whose associated unitary classical structures behave predictably under the transformation, exposing the complex symplectic matrix that dictates the entire thermal equilibrium state and thereby determines its thermal properties.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature.

Let G be an abelian group and A a nonempty subset of G, with elements indexed as $a_0, a_1,..., a_{k-1}$. For any positive integer h less than or equal to k, we can calculate a restricted signed sumset denoted as $h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A$, which comprises sums of $a_i$ with coefficients from the set $\{-1,0,1\}$, where the number of negative coefficients is less than or equal to h and the number of nonnegative coefficients is less than or equal to h-1. Our goal is to find the smallest value of $|h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A|$, given that A consists of k elements in the integers $\mathbb{Z}$, with $|A|\geq3$. We establish that the minimum value of $|h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A|$ is greater than or equal to $|(-1)^{h-1}k^2|$ for all h from 1 to k-1. Conversely, this lower bound is achievable for specific sequences $(a_0,a_1,...,a_{k-1})$ with $(k-1)^2$ congruences modulo $2\cdot k$.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization.

A novel numerical approach has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around analyzing the impact of smoothly varying material inhomogeneities on plane waves. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact propagation direction, solving the time-domain scattering problem, and ultimately deriving the time-harmonic solution via Fourier transformation. Crucial to this approach is a dynamic front-tracking mesh adaptation technique which minimizes the required computational degrees of freedom, thereby enhancing performance by limiting support to the wave front's spatial extent. To complement this strategy, an alternative Fourier transformation-based method is developed, taking advantage of the optimized mesh dimensions to yield a significant improvement in computational efficiency, showcasing the potential for substantial gains (up to three orders of magnitude) over conventional methods. Successful applications and examples illustrate the approach's effectiveness across various scenarios, including heavily inhomogeneous domains with significantly varied material coefficients.

We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three older chondrite finds in Antarctica. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -49. Evaluating various processes on small parent bodies, our analysis suggested minimal water loss during thermal metamorphism, and the water content in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals can be explained by a mixture of D-poor nebular hydrogen and D-rich water from mesostases. Approximately 45-95$\%$ of water with low D isotope values in the pyroxene minerals came from nebular hydrogen, and it's possible that S-type asteroids like 10 Hygiea, with a large surface area, contributed to the delivery of water with low D isotope values to the inner solar system during the accretion period.

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we find exact expressions for scalar products and form factors of higher-spin XXZ chains. This applies to any spin values and mixtures thereof. We verify the affine quantum-group symmetry, $U_q(\hat{sl_2})$, for the XXZ chain's monodromy matrix, enabling exact derivation. Specifically, we use quantum-group symmetry to explicitly obtain diagonalized forms for the B and C operators within the F-basis of the spin-1/2 XXZ chain. This achievement substantiates prior conjectures about the algebraic Bethe-ansatz's correlation function calculations. These results provide a crucial foundation for systematic studies of form factors and correlation functions across solvable models connected to integrable XXZ spin chains.

The growing need for fluent and efficient multilingual communication across languages has intensified the significance of speech-to-text and subsequent text-to-speech translation. Although sequential translation via speech-to-text and text-to-speech has been a established process, the added advantage of direct speech-to-speech translation is expected to improve the translational experience through a more natural medium. Nonetheless, achieving this goal through multilingual models poses significant challenges due to linguistic disparities, limited data availability, and difficulties in learning parallel representations across languages. In this work, a novel, zero-shot speech-to-speech translation framework is introduced, leveraging pre-trained models and learning parallel representations via bilingual contrastive loss. The proposed framework is particularly noteworthy for its ability to process parallel data across languages, thereby enabling the translation of spoken language into foreign languages without prior data. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach on zero-shot speech-to-speech translation tasks through evaluations on LIGUE dataset containing French and Spanish.

We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles composed of semiconductors, dielectrics, and metals over a broad range of wavelengths spanning from the dipolar regime down to the Mie regime.

This study introduces two categories of elements in the algebra U(gl(n)), specifically double Young-Capelli bitableaux and central Schur elements, both displaying remarkable action on the highest weight vectors of irreducible Schur modules. The action results in a new set of elements, P_{\lambda}, linked to the Schur shifted symmetric functions. Notably, P_{\lambda} comprises a product of two elements: the double Young-Capelli bitableaux and a specific element in the center of U(gl(n)), known as the central Schur element. The relationship between P_{\lambda} and the center of U(gl(n)) is intricate and differs from the classical case of gl(1). Furthermore, this study establishes a link between the Schur shifted symmetric functions and quantum immanants, specifically the maximally symmetric quantum immanants. This connection enables the computation of Schur shifted symmetric functions through the evaluation of quantum immanants for specific tableaux.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through loop-level mixing. Furthermore, our analysis of a minimal dark sector composed of weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) delves into the stability of the vacuum, threshold effects, and relic abundance predictions. To ensure the consistency of the model, we set the cutoff beyond 10^11 GeV. Additionally, we identify the parameter region that satisfies the conditions for the vacuum to remain stable, meet the observed WIMP abundance, and comply with direct detection experiments. Moreover, we find the coefficient $R$ (ratio of neutrinoless double beta decay to WIMP-nucleon interaction) in the range of 10^-3 to 10^0, largely depending on the WIMP mass. Consequently, the detection capabilities via neutrinoless double beta decay and direct detection experiments will be crucial in identifying the simplest scoto-seesaw model.

We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling within the context of a single band. The resulting expressions enable a clear understanding of when $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing dominates and when SOE dominates, demifying the commonly held view that $t_{2g}$ dominance only occurs in half-filled shells. Furthermore, we find that SOE can be influenced by electron correlation, leading to additional nuances in the physical properties.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular class of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies.

Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by breaking it down into smaller areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, a method is presented that enables fast computation of Newtonian potentials based on boundary elements, via a sequential reduction of volume integrals into boundary values, involving the application of highly efficient localized approximations for investigating the behavior of harmonics within those elements. This process essentially transforms complex volume computations into simpler boundary computations. The method is highly versatile and can be easily adapted to modify external potentials, solving certain types of volume and boundary integral equations in two dimensions. The proposed algorithm is accompanied by a demonstration of its computational efficiency in solving a scattering problem.
